summary: Researchers have developed WHOLISTIC (WHole-Organism Live-Imaging System for recording Tissue and IntraCellular activity), a new method that images second-timescale cellular activity simultaneously across an entire vertebrate body at cellular resolution. By integrating volumetric fluorescence microscopy, machine learning, and pancellular transgenic expression of calcium sensors in transparent model organisms like larval zebrafish and adult Danionella cerebrum, the system captures complex dynamics spanning multiple organs. This technology bridges cellular and organismal physiology, revealing previously unknown tissue responses and body-wide physiological interactions.
key_points: WHOLISTIC enables simultaneous second-timescale imaging of cellular activity across the entire vertebrate body at cellular resolution.
The method integrates volumetric fluorescence microscopy, advanced image registration algorithms, machine learning, and pancellular transgenic expression of calcium sensors.
It has been successfully demonstrated in larval zebrafish and adult Danionella cerebrum, overcoming the challenge of optical access in opaque tissues.
The technology uncovered novel physiological phenomena, including cold responses in chondrocytes, ketamine responses in meningeal cells, and rhythmic travelling waves along the renal nephron.

title: Just how many species of human have there been? | Discover Wildlife
author: Will Newton
content:
For the last 40,000 years, we (Homo sapiens) have lived alone - the last humans standing from a large and diverse group that, just 300,000 years ago, comprised at least nine species of walking, talking apes.
If you go further back in time you’ll discover even more human species, many of whom followed their own evolutionary paths and gave rise to groups that, while similar, are distinct from humans living today.
- What's the difference between humans and apes? And when did we first appear?
- Why don't humans have fur?
- Early humans may have learnt something from capuchin monkeys
You’d think, given our sense of self-importance, that we’d know a lot about our evolutionary history. This is true to some degree, but in reality we know more about the evolutionary history of other animals than we do our own.
How many human species lived during prehistory?
The study of our evolutionary origins began in the mid-19th century and, since then, we’ve managed to put together a rough family tree.
However, there’s little consensus on exactly how many human species make up this family tree, as new discoveries keep being made and there’s no single, strict definition of human.
If we define ‘human’ as members of the genus Homo, then there are currently 16 recognised species. This is somewhat of a liberal estimate and includes species that may be: (1) known from very few fossils, (2) of uncertain classification, or (3) invalid and better viewed as a synonym of a valid species.
The most familiar species of Homo are, of course, H.sapiens, but there’s also H.neanderthalensis(Neanderthals), H.heidelbergensis, H.erectus, and H.habilis.
The Denisovans are well-known too, though a lot of scientists refer to them as a population (or group) rather than a species. This could change very soon as fossils once thought to belong to other species are now being assigned to the Denisovans.
If we stretch the definition of ‘human’ a bit further and include all of the hominins that evolved after our last common ancestor with chimpanzees and bonobos (who lived around 6.5 million years ago), then there may have been as many as 30 species of human that lived during prehistory!
What was the first human species?
Again, this depends on the definition of ‘human’ you ascribe to.
If we define ‘human’ as members of the genus Homo, then Homo habilis was the first human species. These hairy, forest-dwelling hominids appeared 2.3 million years ago and were the first of our lineage to unequivocally use and manufacture stone tools.
- 5 ancient human species that lived BEFORE us: Meet the prehistoric pioneers who changed history forever
- It turns out we aren't as unique as we think we are: Here are 5 ancient human species that once lived alongside us
If we broaden that definition, then the title of ‘first human species’ is really up for grabs. The 7-million-year-old hominid Sahelanthropus tchadensis may be able to stake a claim, but there’s a suspicion that it may actually be an early ancestor of gorillas rather than humans.
In that case, the title may go to another early hominid, Orrorin tugenenesis (around 6-million-years-old), or Ardipithecus - the first hominid to show definitive signs of a bipedal lifestyle. Ardipithecus lived from 5.8 to 4.3 million years ago and includes two species, A.kadabba and A.ramidus.
summary: For the last 40,000 years, Homo sapiens have been the only surviving human species, though history once included many distinct groups. There is little scientific consensus on the exact number of prehistoric human species due to ongoing discoveries and varying definitions of "human." Depending on whether the definition is limited to the genus Homo or broadened to include all hominins since the last common ancestor with chimpanzees, estimates range from 16 to as many as 30 species.
key_points: Homo sapiens have lived alone as the sole human species for the last 40,000 years.
If defined strictly as members of the genus Homo, there are currently 16 recognised species of human.
Broadening the definition to include all hominins after our split with chimpanzees and bonobos suggests there may have been up to 30 prehistoric human species.
Homo habilis is considered the first human species if using the genus Homo definition, appearing 2.3 million years ago.
Other early hominids like Sahelanthropus tchadensis, Orrorin tugenensis, and Ardipithecus could claim to be the first if broader definitions are used.

title: Underground hydrogen could spur a green-energy revolution — if companies can find it
author: Mitchell Crow; James
content:
In almost 30 countries, energy prospectors are hunting for a potential game changer in the quest to fight global warming. Their quarry is hydrogen gas trapped deep underground in hidden deposits. They hope to find big reservoirs of this geological hydrogen — substantial enough that the gas could become a green replacement for fossil fuels.
![](//media.nature.com/w400/magazine-assets/d41586-026-02850-5/d41586-026-02850-5_23713294.jpg)
How the hydrogen revolution can help save the planet — and how it can’t
When hydrogen is burned to produce electricity, the only by-product is water vapour — no carbon dioxide is emitted. And the potential for geologic hydrogen has energy specialists buzzing. Since 2023, venture capitalists have invested nearly US$500 million in the search for deposits.
A 2024 analysis suggests that Earth’s subsurface probably contains tens of trillions of tonnes of the gas1. If even a small fraction can be recovered at a profit, geologic hydrogen could meet projected clean energy needs for 200 years, potentially at, or even below, the cost of fossil fuels. “That’s why it has gathered momentum as quickly as it has,” says Owain Jackson, head of hydrogen-exploration company H2Au, headquartered in Epsom, UK, which started drilling in Kansas in August.
Or all of this could be a pipe dream. Nobody knows whether there are large enough deposits of geological hydrogen to match the hype. That’s why companies are racing to drill into the ground in many geological formations, from northern Canada to eastern Africa to South Australia. Findings from these wells could emerge within the next few months, providing key clues about the potential for geologic hydrogen.
“At the moment, we still don’t know if it’s almost nothing or completely everywhere,” says David Waltham, a geophysicist at Royal Holloway, University of London.
Unknown resource
All this excitement caught geologists by surprise. “On Wikipedia, natural hydrogen didn’t exist five years ago,” Jackson says.
Why didn’t hydrogen exploration begin decades ago? “Quite literally because everyone assumed it wasn’t there,” says Waltham.
That was true even for researchers studying hydrogen produced inside the Earth: the idea that the gas could accumulate underground to form large deposits never occurred to them, says geologist Chris Ballentine at the University of Oxford, UK.
The basic geochemistry of hydrogen production is well established2. The gas forms when iron-rich igneous rock, such as olivine, reacts with water. It can also be generated when α-particles, emitted by the radioactive decay of uranium or thorium, hit water molecules and split them. When hydrogen produced by these processes seeps through rock towards the surface, it can support subterranean microbial communities.
“I’ve been looking at the types of geological systems that produce natural hydrogen for quite some time — from the perspective of an energy source for microbes, not for society,” says Ballentine.
![](//media.nature.com/w400/magazine-assets/d41586-026-02850-5/d41586-026-02850-5_53696730.jpg)
EU leaders should not rush to revamp green-hydrogen rules
Researchers assumed that hydrogen produced underground wouldn’t accumulate in geological deposits that could be tapped.
“The Earth is a machine that produces huge volumes of hydrogen — but it is also a machine that destroys huge volumes of hydrogen,” says Eric Gaucher at Lavoisier H2 Geoconsult in Chamonix, France, who co-leads the natural-hydrogen taskforce at the International Energy Agency, based in Paris. That’s because microbes use the gas, and it is also consumed by geochemical reactions. Geologists assumed that any hydrogen that escapes that fate would leak through rock layers and disappear into the atmosphere, because the molecules are too small to become trapped underground, beneath impermeable rock layers.
Some geologists started to question that assumption in 2018. That’s when researchers published a report describing the discovery of a substantial hydrogen deposit in Mali3. “The first time it hit the scientific literature, it caught our attention,” Ballentine says. Geologists reasoned that bigger deposits of hydrogen could be out there, waiting to be found.
There is another line of evidence supporting this view: hydrogen can accumulate in deep mines — where it must be pumped out to avoid explosion. In 2024, for example, researchers found that at least 200 tonnes of hydrogen is released annually from a chromite mine in Albania, one of the biggest natural flow rates of hydrogen ever recorded4.
Getting the gas
Finding substantial deposits of hydrogen underground could revive hopes for a hydrogen economy — a possible future in which the gas would replace fossil fuels in many applications. Proponents have long touted the idea of using renewable energy to split water and generate hydrogen for producing electricity and powering clean vehicles. But hydrogen has so far proven prohibitively expensive, and there is scepticism about how big of an impact hydrogen energy can make.
If cheap and plentiful geologic hydrogen exists, it could change all that. Although the geologic processes that produce hydrogen are slow and it is a relatively finite resource, estimates suggest that there could be enough already accumulated in underground reserves to provide the world with sufficient time to find alternative sources of energy that don’t contribute to climate change. But first, researchers have to answer many questions, including how quickly hydrogen forms under different geological conditions, how it migrates through rock, where it might accumulate and how long it persists once trapped.
summary: Energy prospectors across nearly 30 countries are searching for natural hydrogen trapped deep underground as a potential green replacement for fossil fuels. While a 2024 analysis suggests Earth's subsurface could contain vast amounts of the gas, researchers still do not know if large, extractable deposits actually exist. Companies are currently racing to drill wells worldwide, with findings expected in the coming months that will determine the viability of geologic hydrogen.
key_points: Venture capitalists have invested nearly US$500 million since 2023 to search for underground hydrogen deposits.
A 2024 analysis indicates Earth's subsurface may hold tens of trillions of tonnes of hydrogen.
Natural hydrogen is formed through geochemical reactions involving iron-rich rocks or radioactive decay interacting with water.
Historically, geologists assumed hydrogen could not accumulate in underground deposits because it would leak or be consumed by microbes.
The discovery of a substantial deposit in Mali in 2018 and ongoing gas releases in mines have renewed interest in finding large reserves.

title: Should we still admire Stephen Hawking?
author: Simon Ings
content:
![Prof Stephen Hawking photographed at the Centre for Mathematical Sciences, University of Cambridge](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/books/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000157380963_17889593110725_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqg0QhGUrJBLC1cMiJLC7a776Xj2WECU5tGTp4vDMBGsY.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Prof Stephen Hawking photographed at the Centre for Mathematical Sciences, University of Cambridge](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/books/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000157380963_17889593110725_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqg0QhGUrJBLC1cMiJLC7a776Xj2WECU5tGTp4vDMBGsY.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Eight years have passed since the theoretical physicist Stephen Hawking died, aged 76, of complications caused by motor neurone disease (MND). It was a condition that everyone expected would kill him in his mid-20s. Hawking faced down his gathering weakness and paralysis from a “ghastly prison”, as Graham Farmelo puts it in Hawking: His Life and Work, and from there issued, over 50 years, an extraordinary stream of intellectual accomplishments.
At the beginning of his career, in the midst of trying to understand the Big Bang – the “starting singularity” from which both time and space emerged – Hawking also, by-the-by, predicted just about everything we’ve since observed about black holes. His popular science writing made him into a celebrity: A Brief History of Time (1988) was a bestseller, and broke a record for appearing on the Sunday Times charts for 264 weeks. His funeral was attended variously by Eddie Redmayne (who played him in the 2014 biopic, The Theory of Everything), Brian Cox, and, perhaps not so curiously, Elon Musk.
No one has ever been so crass to suggest that Hawking’s accomplishments could ever redeem the ghastliness of his disease – but they serve as testament to the willpower of a man who had every reason to doubt that there was a special meaning to human life.
Hawking was born on January 8 1942 with an “enormous head”, according to his mother, Isobel, and “one of the loudest voices I’ve ever heard”. His sister Mary quickly found him to be “one of the most self-centred people I’ve ever met”. He stood out at St Albans School in 1952, if only for his ineptitude and physical awkwardness, and, at 17, entered University College, Oxford, where he coasted through his three-year degree by doing an average of an hour of work a day.
Hawking’s friends nicknamed him “Moomin”, because he was intensely excited by everything and constantly getting into scrapes. Indeed, in his second year, as the early symptoms of his MND began to manifest, he suffered a terrifying fall down a 30ft wooden college staircase. Hawking was so afraid that he might have sustained brain damage from the incident that he took to falling asleep at night to a tape loop of his own voice endlessly reassuring him: “You are a genius.”
The scientist met his future wife, Jane Wilde, an English teacher, at a New Year’s party in 1962, just as he was beginning postgraduate research at Cambridge and shortly before he was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), the most common and least forgiving form of MND. Knowing this, the couple married in 1965 and had three children.
![Stephen Hawking and his wife, Jane Wilde](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/books/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000270734957_178895931103811_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq-GHjhXop0Qdah32PeEutV8u5Oty4bSuNC9xmdb-t5AM.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Hawking’s mother never felt easy about their life together. As early as 1970, when Hawking resorted to a wheelchair for the first time, she wrote in her journal: “I don’t know whether the Stephen-Jane business is a happy defiance of the fates, or an unnatural pretence, whether there is real value in it or only a stubborn refusal to believe in the tragedy of life.”
That “stubborn refusal” led Hawking and Jane through a series of ever-evolving, ever-more dysfunctional domestic arrangements. In 1977, as Hawking’s condition deteriorated, Jane brought family friend Jonathan Hellyer Jones into the house to help her care for her husband. He became her lover, while Hawking grew ever closer to Elaine Mason, his nurse. Jane and Hawking’s parents fell out horribly.
The emotional gimcrackery of this arrangement blew up in everyone’s face once Hawking divorced Jane and married Elaine in 1995. The Sun and The Daily Mail ran sensational pieces about Elaine’s alleged abuse of her new husband, and the police even got involved (the couple strongly denied the allegations and the police dropped their investigation in 2004). When this second marriage ended in divorce, Hawking was left helpless, having to spend his nights alone – something he naturally abhorred. Newspapers reported that he fell for another of his carers, Diana King, who was 39 years his junior. Farmelo doesn’t give the story the time of day.
![Stephen Hawking and Elaine Mason on their wedding day in 1995](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/books/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000501548624_17889593116182_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqrzaGM-vBq4k2SYQUDLkBHhL4HJrsjDQ_1mY3Ee0kSYw.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
He never quite clarifies whether Hawking went to Jeffrey Epstein’s island, Little St James. We’re told only that Hawking went to the nearby St Thomas for a conference partly sponsored by the sex offender in March 2006. As for the notorious photo of Hawking surrounded by bikini-clad women sipping cocktails, Farmelo says that it was taken in Florida, and “had no connection with Epstein… It is unclear how the photo came to be included in the files.”
Still, Farmelo’s “authorised” biography is no snow job. His portrait acknowledges that Hawking was never an especially nice person. Hawking was more than happy to point this out himself: in The Simpsons episode “They Saved Lisa’s Brain”, broadcast in May 1999, Hawking – and it really is Hawking – says to Homer: “Your theory of a doughnut-shaped universe is intriguing. I may have to steal it.” (Farmelo’s access to the family archive enables him to explore several intellectual feuds between Hawking and other scientists over attribution, though they aren’t what you could call juicy.)
![Stephen Hawking at Princeton in 1979](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/books/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000501548521_17889593110174_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq8juO8C_Vdx2cT20LARTibnFLfv0ucAwTrkjYdq767p4.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The more pressing concern is whether we need another biography at all. Farmelo wants us to look past Hawking the Man to understand Hawking the Project: a determined mass effort, extending across decades, to maintain one human spirit against huge physical odds. But there are already glimpses of that project in Jane’s Music to Move the Stars (1999), expanded eight years later into Travelling to Infinity: My Life with Stephen. More recently, in 2021, we had Charles Seife’s very good Hawking Hawking: The Selling of a Scientific Celebrity.
Farmelo spends early chapters dutifully paying homage to every family connection. But the book does eventually get going, and he handles Hawking’s scientific accomplishments with trademark economy and precision. His main achievement is to bring something of Isobel Hawking’s unsparing clear-sightedness to his warmly sympathetic account: Hawking’s relationship with his melancholy, self-pitying father disintegrated over years; Farmelo calls it a “waste of love”.
And there’s genuine outrage simmering under his account of how Hawking destroyed the career and confidence of his young graduate student Andrew Farley, who dared to claim that – contrary to Hawking’s view – information is not lost in black holes.
Farmelo meets head-on the challenge set by a subject who, having lived an entire life under an immediate death sentence, has already worked out its punchline. It was one Hawking got so fed up repeating to people, he even pre-programmed it into his computer: “It’s not as if I had a choice and deliberately chose a difficult path,” he would say, through the machine that, after a tracheostomy in 1985, enabled him to speak. “I have just done the only thing open to me in the situation.”
★★★★☆
Hawking: His Life and Work is published by John Murray at £30. To order your copy for £25, call 0330 173 0523 or visit Telegraph Books
summary: Stephen Hawking achieved extraordinary scientific accomplishments over a 50-year career despite facing a severe, life-limiting diagnosis of motor neurone disease in his 20s. Graham Farmelo's biography, "Hawking: His Life and Work," presents an unsparing portrait that explores both his intellectual legacy and the complex, often difficult personal realities of his life. The book examines Hawking's marriages, his celebrity status, his scientific feuds, and the collective effort required to sustain him through decades of physical decline.
key_points: Stephen Hawking was diagnosed with motor neurone disease in his early 20s, yet lived to the age of 76.
He made groundbreaking predictions about black holes and achieved global fame with his bestseller A Brief History of Time.
Graham Farmelo's biography addresses Hawking's personal flaws, complex domestic life, and various intellectual feuds rather than offering a purely hagiographic account.
The biography highlights Hawking as a "project," detailing the immense collaborative effort required to sustain his spirit and work against severe physical odds.

title: This lake in Canada just vanished. And it's not coming back. | Discover Wildlife
author: Will Newton
content:
A new study has confirmed what researchers have feared since the breakup of the Milne Ice Shelf in 2020: Canada’s last epishelf lake – a freshwater lake dammed by an ice shelf – has gone.
Drawing on a decade of ocean measurements, satellite images, and field observations collected before and after the breakup, scientists have reconstructed the lake’s disappearance.
- Arctic bobtail squid seen alive in natural habitat for first time ever
- 100km-wide "hidden giant" discovered beneath Antarctic ice sheet
The far north of Canada lies in the Arctic Circle and serves as one of the region’s last refuges for summer sea ice and ice-dependent wildlife, such as polar bears, ringed seals, and Atlantic walruses.
In the local Inuktitut language, these protected areas on northern Ellesmere Island in Nunavut are known as Tuvaijuittuq, ‘the place where ice never melts’.
Only, the ice is melting. The recent loss of the Milne Fiord epishelf lake – a millennia-old ecosystem and the last of its kind in Canada – has demonstrated that even this once seemingly permanent ice refuge is vulnerable to the rapid changes associated with a warming climate.
- 11 Arctic animals that thrive in this inhospitable freezing landscape
- Why can't polar bears live in Antarctica?
![Weather station and and tent on the ice shelf](https://www.discoverwildlife.com/resources/content/f347d34d-c1a6-4a00-b570-b78c2dcb3211/24885197-9f29-4a26-a76e-c9b3fb8b7f7f/39643ed5-734d-4916-97d3-acb7a2fe3c47/Weather-station-and-and-tent-on-the-ice-shelf-scaled.jpeg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=aa09b403-68ea-4659-a84e-92471d7ed6be)
At the end of August, a study published in Scientific Reports by a team of researchers from the University of British Columbia (UBC), University of Alberta, Université Laval, and Carleton University pulled together many different lines of evidence and demonstrated that the epishelf lake started draining as soon as the Milne Ice Shelf broke apart in July 2020.
By autumn 2020, the epishelf lake and the unique ecosystem it supported had mostly vanished.
“The ice shelf and lake had been thinning for decades, but the 2020 breakup was the last straw. The lake drained within months,” said the study’s lead author Jérémie Bonneau, who conducted part of the research during his PhD at UBC.
An epishelf lake forms when an ice shelf acts as a dam, trapping a layer of freshwater floating above seawater connected to the ocean. These kinds of lakes create multi-story habitats that allow freshwater and marine wildlife to coexist within the same water column.
![Milne Ice Shelf breakup](https://www.discoverwildlife.com/resources/content/f347d34d-c1a6-4a00-b570-b78c2dcb3211/24885197-9f29-4a26-a76e-c9b3fb8b7f7f/cd2878ff-5565-4366-bdcd-37760bd400a0/Milne-Ice-Shelf-breakup-scaled.jpeg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=aa09b403-68ea-4659-a84e-92471d7ed6be)
The first field measurements collected after the breakup in 2020 showed that, by July 2022, brackish water had fully replaced the lake’s distinct freshwater layer. Since then, annual monitoring has shown no signs of recovery, suggesting the lake has gone for good.
“Epishelf lakes can signal when an ice shelf is under stress, and that’s what we saw here,” said co-author Bernard Laval. “The data showed the ice shelf was failing. Once the ice is gone, the ecosystem goes with it. There’s no coming back.”
Studying dynamic systems such as these in one of the most remote parts of the world is no easy task.
To reach Milne Fiord, researchers had to take multiple flights to Ottawa, Iqaluit, and then Resolute Bay, via Arctic Bay. In Resolute Bay, they spent several days at the federal Polar Continental Shelf Program Base, preparing equipment before a light aircraft, known as a Twin Otter, took them the rest of the way.
Once there, the researchers planted sensor tubes about the size of thermoses, recording temperature, depth and conductivity, which they used to determine the water’s salt content. These instruments were left in place during the COVID-cancelled 2020 field season and weren’t able to be retrieved until two years later.
- How the COVID lockdown accidentally created an incredible nature experiment
- Can any animals survive freezing?
![Laval retrieving a mooring in a Milne Ice Shelf pond](https://www.discoverwildlife.com/resources/content/f347d34d-c1a6-4a00-b570-b78c2dcb3211/24885197-9f29-4a26-a76e-c9b3fb8b7f7f/dd0baa9a-3827-424b-b71e-d7246227d902/Laval-retrieving-a-mooring-in-a-Milne-Ice-Shelf-pond.jpeg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=aa09b403-68ea-4659-a84e-92471d7ed6be)
“We saw the [Milne Ice Shelf] breakup on satellite images, and two years later we got the data,” said Laval. “The instruments were there, observing. We just couldn’t reach them.”
The study found that freshwater entering Milne Fiord is now flushed directly into the ocean as the remaining ice shelf can no longer contain it. For the lake to re-establish itself, the ice shelf would need to recover – something the researchers say is an impossibility given the current climate trajectory.
“These systems took thousands of years to form and were lost in months,” said Bonneau. “On any human timescale, they are not coming back.”
You can read more about the study published in Scientific Reports here.
Top image: As the Milne Ice Shelf fractured, it exposed freshwater channels that once lay protected beneath the surface. Credit: Cameron Fitzpatrick

- It's one of the oldest and driest deserts in the world, is 5 times drier than the Sahara – and it's about to bloom with millions of flowers
- People started building artificial beaver dams in California. Now something "mind blowing" is happening

summary: A new scientific study has confirmed that Canada's last epishelf lake has completely disappeared following the breakup of the Milne Ice Shelf in July 2020. Located on northern Ellesmere Island, the millennia-old freshwater ecosystem drained within months and was replaced by brackish water by 2022. Researchers state that the lake shows no signs of recovery and will not return under current climate conditions.
key_points: Canada's last epishelf lake, dammed by the Milne Ice Shelf, vanished after the shelf broke apart in July 2020.
The millennia-old freshwater ecosystem drained within months and was fully replaced by brackish water by July 2022.
Annual monitoring shows no signs of recovery, and researchers indicate the lake is gone for good.
Epishelf lakes serve as multi-story habitats allowing freshwater and marine wildlife to coexist within the same water column.

title: Multivariate MOFs make the case for embracing complexity
author: Mason Wakley
content:
Frameworks built from multiple different metals and ligands are expanding the possibilities for materials that can do many things at once
Omar Yaghi is convinced that chemists should embrace complexity. ‘Right now, materials in general have one structure, one property, one operation,’ he says. ‘[Yet] it would be great if we could design materials… where several things are happening at once.’
This is surprising for a chemist who helped establish the field of metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), a contribution recognised by last year’s Nobel prize in chemistry, which Yaghi shared with Susumu Kitagawa and Richard Robson. Yet in recent years, Yaghi has moved away from creating conventional MOFs built from a single type of linker and metal node. Instead, he and other chemists have found ways to incorporate multiple organic ligands and different metal building blocks within a single structure.
It would be great if we could design materials… where several things are happening at once
This new class of materials – known as multivariate- or MTV-MOFs – drastically expands the scope and capability of porous frameworks. ‘[Chemists] look at [MTV-MOFs] and they say “Oh my God, this is just in one structure? You have too many things happening”,’ says Yaghi. ‘A lot of people shy away from it [but] I think that [it’s] a big opportunity to transform our chemistry.’
MTV-MOFs allow chemists to create materials that have pores of various sizes and chemistries, which often leads to structures with multiple functions. This could be, for example, a material that captures carbon dioxide in one part of a framework and then uses the bound molecules in a catalytic reaction in another region.
Yaghi notes that these materials take inspiration from nature, which thrives on combining multiple building blocks together for a specific function. Collections of different amino acids decorate an enzyme’s active site, for example, producing a finely tuned catalyst. Similarly, having a mixture of metals and ligands within an MTV-MOF could help control the function and specificity of these materials. Combining a range of building blocks also drastically increases ‘the possibilities of different compounds being made with different combinations,’ Yaghi explains.
Neil Champness at the University of Birmingham, UK, shares Yaghi’s enthusiasm for these materials. ‘There were already enormous numbers of MOFs, but [these multivariate materials] basically take the cap off… [it’s] essentially an infinite number.’ While for many chemists this may seem daunting, Champness thinks, like Yaghi, that chemists should embrace complexity. ‘You can make 1000 different MOFs until you’ve found the one which is right, or you [can] make a multivariate system that does the reaction anyway.’
Making MTV-MOFs
In 2010, Yaghi’s team at the University of California, Berkeley in the US produced one of the first MTV-MOFs by reacting zinc oxide clusters with functionalised terephthalic acid linkers. This led to a series of materials that had up to eight different organic ligands in one structure.1 ‘Typically in inorganic chemistry… when you have multiple building blocks coming together, you make multiple compounds,’ Yaghi explains. He describes realising that these framework materials don’t behave in the same way as a ‘big discovery’. This prompted Yaghi’s team to propose a new class of materials, which is when they coined the term MTV-MOFs to describe them.
Fifteen years later, his team has now created several MTV-MOFs, some of which have up to 36 different ligands.2 Yaghi’s group noted at the time that this particular material had a ‘record number of linkers and functionalities’ in a single framework. This may seem like an exercise in seeing just how complex these materials can become. But the team think that MTV-MOFs with this number of linkers could help chemists quickly identify which ligands or combinations thereof work best for a specific application. This drastically cuts the number of homogeneous MOFs that chemists would need to make, saving time and resources.
Yaghi’s team was able to synthesise such MTV-MOFs using similar methods to typical framework materials. This involves heating multiple linkers with metal building blocks in solution for several days, before repeatedly washing the crystals with solvent. Adjusting the ratio of the linkers and metals then allows chemists to create different MTV-MOFs.
However, this method doesn’t work for all MTV-MOF structures. For example, certain frameworks are challenging to make from scratch as introducing multiple ligands can affect their solubility or cause linkers to compete for interactions with metal nodes.
Chemists have since found alternative ways to synthesise these materials. Seth Cohen at the University of San Diego in the US says that as ‘these [framework] materials are just basically acting like big coordination compounds’, chemists can exploit this property to make MTV-MOFs. This involves swapping out organic linkers within a pre-made framework – a technique known as postsynthetic ligand exchange. Typically, this is limited to replacing one linker with an organic molecule of a similar length and connectivity, as this helps maintain the MOF’s overall structure. Cohen adds that this process usually occurs from the outside-in, which can create layers that have different linkers. Leaving the reaction for longer would eventually replace all ligands, creating a different but homogenous MOF, rather than an MTV-MOF.
His team showed that this technique could work back in 2012 by swapping out the brominated ligands in a zirconium-based MOF for an amino-functionalised linker.3 Reacting the homogeneous amino- and brominated-MOF structures together also led to a MOF containing both linkers, as the ligands of either MOF partially exchanged.
Rather than swapping out ligands, chemists are also able to chemically modify the linkers themselves. Cohen’s team, for example, was able to react amino-functionalised ligands with anhydrides of various chain lengths, with conversion rates ranging from 11 to 99%.4 ‘Basically, any time we had a post-synthetic modification reaction on a ligand that didn’t go to completion, by definition, we had created a multivariate MOF,’ says Cohen.
These modifications allowed the group to alter the hydrophobicity of a zinc-based MOF, as well as its internal surface area. Synthesising these materials in this way ensured ‘reliable access to a family of closely related MOFs,’ the group noted, which made it easier to compare material properties. Ligand modification also works for various other functional groups, including azide click reactions5 to incorporate fluorescent tags or Schiff base reactions with amines.6
What are multivariate metal-organic frameworks?
A quick introduction to why complexity is the next challenge for MOF materials
What is a metal-organic-framework (MOF?)
MOFs are 3D network materials made of metal ions or clusters connected by organic linkers. They are often highly porous, with voids that can capture molecules selectively, making them useful in a wide variety of applications such as separations, sensing, gas storage and catalysis.
		
![Example MOF](https://d2fc7ojl9ttfsq.cloudfront.net/CMS/s3/rscedu-library/web/r/t/d/image4_838879.png?w=714) 
What is a multivariate MOF (MTV-MOF)?
Conventional MOFs typically contain a single type of metal node and linker, but MTV-MOFs incorporate multiple linkers and nodes. The result is a material that combines an ordered framework with chemical heterogeneity.
		
![Example MOF](https://d2fc7ojl9ttfsq.cloudfront.net/CMS/s3/rscedu-library/web/r/t/d/image3_122596.jpg?w=726) 
How do you make MTV-MOFs?
The simplest way is to mix the metals and linkers in a solvent, then heat, just like a normal MOF. Researchers often select linkers with similar shapes but different functional groups, thereby introducing extra functionality without changing the framework structure.
You can also make a MOF first and then modify it in various ways:
- Ligand exchange can be used to replace linkers with new ones
- Metal exchange can swap out some of the metal ions with different metals
- Chemical modification can transform functional groups on some of the linkers
Why are chemists excited by these materials?
MTV-MOFs offer a way to introduce complexity into highly ordered materials, mimicking the kind of controlled complexity found in biological systems.
An MTV-MOF could, for example, capture a molecule in one part of the framework and transform it chemically in another, allowing several functions to operate within a single material.
Is that as simple as it sounds?
No, it’s much harder. The feature that makes MTV-MOFs attractive also makes them difficult to study: complexity.
		
![Multivariate MOF](https://d2fc7ojl9ttfsq.cloudfront.net/CMS/s3/rscedu-library/web/q/h/r/webchemistryworldmof15x15thrcopy_509435.png?w=944) 
Like conventional crystalline MOFs, MTV-MOFs retain an ordered framework, but there is chemical diversity within it, blurring the line between order and disorder.
The lack of uniform composition means they are also much harder to characterise – the local composition varies across the material in ways that can be hard to predict.
Give me some examples
      ![Example MOF](https://d2fc7ojl9ttfsq.cloudfront.net/CMS/s3/rscedu-library/web/r/t/d/image1_504221.png?w=1000) 
      ![Image 1 portrait](https://d2fc7ojl9ttfsq.cloudfront.net/CMS/s3/rscedu-library/web/p/q/l/image1portrait_140537.png?w=665) 
MTV-MOF-74 is based on a framework in which divalent metal ions are linked by 2,5-dioxidoterephthalate. It can contain up to 10 different metal ions and chemists can tune its overall composition to alter its properties. For example, introducing Ni2+ or Co2+ into Mg-MOF-74 can improve its stability in water.
      ![Example MOF](https://d2fc7ojl9ttfsq.cloudfront.net/CMS/s3/rscedu-library/web/r/t/d/image2_986793.png?w=1000) 
      ![Image 2 portrait](https://d2fc7ojl9ttfsq.cloudfront.net/CMS/s3/rscedu-library/web/p/q/l/image2portrait_623625.png?w=801) 
MOF-303/MIL-160 combines two linkers, 3,5-pyrazoledicarboxylic acid from MOF-303 and 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid from MIL-160, with aluminium-based nodes. MOF-303 provides high carbon dioxide uptake, while MIL-160 offers stronger carbon dioxide selectivity. By combining both features, the MTVMOF achieves improved carbon dioxide separation from methane compared with either parent material.
All pictures © SciComm Studio/Anna Tanczos
Mixing metals
‘Now, with [exchanging] metals, it’s a little bit different,’ explains Cohen. Metal ions have different sizes, coordination numbers and coordination geometries. To keep the MOF structure intact, chemists are often limited to exchanging metal ions with ones that form stronger bonds with a given organic linker. This typically follows the Irving–Williams series, such that Cu(II) ions can swap out Zn(II) ions, but not the other way around.
Natalia Shustova and her research group at the University of South Carolina in the US recently used this strategy to create a photocatalytic copper-based MOF from its zinc precursor.7 To do this, the team immersed a zinc-based MOF in a copper nitrate solution, resulting in around 95% of the zinc ions transmetallating with copper cations.
Exposing the mixed-metal framework to ultraviolet light caused electrons to transfer from a photoactive spiropyran linker to the copper cations. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy revealed that the MTV-MOF had a combination of Cu(II) and Cu(I) cations. These metal sites were then able to work together to catalyse the coupling reaction between an aldehyde, azide and aminated pyridine to form a variety of commodity chemicals and pharmaceuticals, such as the drug zolpidem, which is used to treat insomnia. Achieving this would not have been possible in a zinc-based framework as its d10 electron configuration makes the metal catalytically inactive, Shustova says. However, synthesising the copper-based framework from scratch is challenging. Swapping out zinc ions for copper cations allows the team to get the desired catalytic properties from a known zinc-based material.
Champness’s group has also been experimenting with making framework materials with multiple metals. In a recent preprint, his team reported how it had introduced all the lanthanide elements into a single structure.8 ‘We were doing it purely from a curiosity point of view,’ Champness says. Even so, as lanthanides fluoresce in the UV, visible and near-infrared regions of the electromagnetic spectrum, these elements are useful as biological imaging agents, for example. Introducing multiple metals into a framework and varying their concentrations could create new materials with tuneable emissive properties, says Champness. Such materials combine the useful properties of multiple lanthanides, rather than being limited to MOFs with a singular function.
However, Champness explains that although the team reacted various lanthanide ions in a one-to-one ratio, this did not necessarily lead to the same metal ratios in the final product. Trivalent lanthanides have similar coordination properties, but they decrease in size across the period. This leads to a preference for smaller cations with higher charge density to the metal nodes within the framework, as they bind more strongly to the organic linkers.
Scanning electron microscopy helped Champness’s team probe which metals cations were in the structure, as well as their location, while advanced mass spectrometry determined their quantity. ‘How those metals order through the MOF is completely variable within our systems,’ explains Champness. ‘It’s entirely random as far as we can tell.’
Chemists can also use other techniques to probe the structure of these multivariate materials. High resolution solution and solid-state NMR can help determine the ratio of linkers, for example, while x-ray diffraction experiments reveal the material’s overall bulk structure. However, these analytical methods have drawbacks, such as overlapping signals from similar ligands. Reduced signal intensity, owing to less of each metal or linker in such frameworks, can also make it challenging to fully assign peaks and characterise these materials.
The experiments to characterise these materials can also be time consuming and difficult. For example, Yaghi’s team has previously used a technique known as atom probe tomography to map the metal sequences in mixed-metal MOFs.9 Laser pulses sequentially evaporate the ions at the material’s surface on to a detector, which then analyses the ion’s mass-to-charge ratio. This allowed the team to construct a 3D map of the framework. The team found that metals were, relative to each other, either randomly positioned, clustered or inserted sparingly throughout the framework, depending on the specific combination of metals and reaction temperature.
However, ‘shaving’ each of the layers of the materials, analysing them individually and using this technique for large numbers of materials is going to be difficult, notes Champness.
‘As scientists, we tend to like to know the answer to everything,’ says Champness. ‘[But] you could ask the question: “Do you need to know what the [exact] structure is?”’ If chemists synthesise a multivariate framework with a specific property – perhaps one that catalyses a certain reaction or interacts with a specific molecule – and can reproduce the property each time, then knowing the local structure of these materials is less important, Champness argues. He likens it to polymer chemistry, where chemists don’t always know the exact ordering of monomers and instead care about the overall properties of the polymer itself.
‘There is essentially a cost–benefit analysis at some point,’ says Champness. ‘Working out local structure is time consuming and difficult, so there needs to be a reason for doing it… Sometimes there is [and] sometimes there isn’t.’ Understanding the local structure might be relevant if a material has an unusual or unexpected property, for example.
Computing complexity
Using computational methods to design, study and analyse MTV-MOFs could help researchers understand how multiple linkers and metal cations combine, without needing to carry out hands-on experiments. Yaghi points out that even a small set of metal nodes and linkers can generate an incomprehensible number of possible MTV-MOFs. Diversity arises not only from the choice of building blocks, but also from the many ways they can be combined. As a result, ‘we’re not going to madly be making one MOF after another’, he says.
Emma Wolpert at University College London, UK, explains that ‘computational models can generate different possible arrangements of metals, linkers, defects or domains, and then test which models are consistent with the experimental data’.
‘For example, we can compare simulated and experimental diffraction patterns, … spectroscopic signatures or measured properties. This can help distinguish between a truly random mixture, correlated disorder [or] clustering,’ she adds.
However, Wolpert recognises that while thermodynamics primarily guides the creation of such materials, solvent, kinetics and different crystal growth pathways all affect the final structure. ‘Computational methods can address some of these effects, but they are much more difficult, system-specific and not yet routine for high-throughput design,’ she says.
‘I would think that [artificial intelligence (AI)] for something like multivariate MOFs could be super valuable,’ says Cohen. He explains that AI tools could help chemists figure out synthetic conditions, synthetic strategies and ligand modifications that would create a certain structure. ‘AI can really find parameters and data that you wouldn’t think about being correlated with a certain property,’ he adds.
While computational and AI models will likely change how chemists study these materials, MTV-MOFs will also influence synthetic approaches. Yaghi notes that controlling the temperature, the quantity and purity of starting materials and other reaction conditions will be critical, for example. ‘[These multivariate materials are] going to require chemistry to be even more rigorous than we are [currently] to produce the same material [each time],’ he says. This will be crucial when scaling up and producing these materials at the commercial level, he notes.
Finding applications
‘A lot of very important chemical transformations, [like] the challenges of turning carbon dioxide into something useful, becomes an interesting possibility,’ with MTV-MOFs, says Yaghi. He points out the resemblance of these materials to biological enzymes, owing to the pores acting like active sites.
In 2016, Yaghi and his team were able to create an enzyme-like MTV-MOF, which could selectively cleave specific peptide bonds as efficiently as the enzyme TEV protease.10 Synthesising a magnesium-based MOF with protected amine groups allowed the team to introduce several tripeptide amino acid sequences into the MOF’s pores. The amino acids are similar to those found in the biological enzyme. ‘We just sort of threw [the amino acids] in there, onto the skeleton, and we found that this MOF does exactly what the enzyme does,’ says Yaghi.
The simplicity of the idea drags you in … and you get sucked into this whirlpool of possibilities
Aside from capturing biological-like activity in synthetic materials, Yaghi’s team has also created MTV-MOFs to harvest water from the atmosphere, even in desert regions with low humidity.11 The team has developed a series of aluminium-based MTV-MOFs by varying the ratio of two organic ligands during synthesis: a dicarboxylate thiophene and a dicarboxylate pyrazole. Increasing the proportion of pyrazole linkers makes it more energetically favourable for water molecules to adsorb at lower humidities. Equally, MOFs that have a higher proportion of thiophene can desorb water at lower temperatures, such as at night. Balancing the ratio of these linkers has led to an MTV-MOF with optimised properties, which the team has scaled up to produce several kilograms in one batch with yields reaching up to 90%. Yaghi’s team has recently filed a patent for this material.
For Yaghi, this water-harvesting material represents a shift from chemists simply making, characterising and studying a material, to pushing compounds ‘all the way to commercialisation’. ‘That would be what a chemistry lab would [now] be doing – not just making the molecule and the material but also integrating that material into a device.’
Expanding the scope of these multivariate frameworks is going to require collaboration between chemists, as well as material scientists, biologists, mathematicians and physicists. ‘I think the beauty of MOFs is that almost anybody with a chemistry degree can come up with an idea for a new [structure],’ says Champness. ‘The simplicity of the idea drags you in, and then there’s endless complexity, and you kind of get sucked into this whirlpool of possibilities.’ For Champness, ‘multivariate [MOFs] are just kind of an extension of that experience’.

summary: Multivariate metal-organic frameworks (MTV-MOFs) incorporate multiple types of metal nodes and organic linkers into a single ordered structure, expanding the capabilities of conventional porous materials. By embracing chemical complexity, these materials can perform multiple functions simultaneously, such as capturing carbon dioxide and catalyzing chemical reactions. Chemists synthesize MTV-MOFs either by mixing various building blocks directly in solution or through post-synthetic methods like ligand and metal exchange. Although their heterogeneous composition makes them more challenging to characterize and study, MTV-MOFs offer vast potential for tailoring specific material properties.
key_points: MTV-MOFs integrate multiple organic ligands and metal building blocks into a single structured framework, moving beyond conventional single-component MOFs.
Combining diverse building blocks allows a single material to perform multiple functions, such as simultaneous gas capture and catalysis.
Chemists can synthesize MTV-MOFs by heating various linkers and metals together in solution or by altering pre-made frameworks using techniques like ligand and metal exchange.
The chemical diversity and varying local composition of MTV-MOFs make them significantly harder to characterize and study than traditional homogeneous materials.

title: Five night sky events to look forward to this autumn
author: Emily Wood
content:
![The November full moon shines bright white in a black sky, with the outline of tree branches in the foreground.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/902/cpsprodpb/aff8/live/ce59c3a0-ad0f-11f1-a035-c91dffce51bf.jpg)
This year's November full Moon will appear as a supermoon. This is 2025's November Beaver Moon captured above forests in Hungary
- Published
Autumn brings longer nights to the northern hemisphere, offering more opportunities to get outside and look up at the night sky.
There is plenty to look out for over the coming months, from impressive meteor showers to dazzling star clusters.
The series of spectacles begins with the Pleiades as the autumn nights draw in.
It will be followed by the impressive Orionid meteor shower in late October, and a planetary parade, the Leonid meteor shower and a supermoon in November.
The Pleiades
![A group of stars shine bright white in the middle of starry black night sky.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/905/cpsprodpb/4605/live/00715870-ad16-11f1-826f-933990eae6f0.jpg)
A view of the Pleiades star cluster, also known as the Seven Sisters or Messier 45 (M45)
As the nights lengthen through autumn, one of the most recognisable star clusters in the night sky becomes increasingly prominent.
The Pleiades, also known as the Seven Sisters, is a cluster of young stars around 440 light years from Earth.
Despite its name, most people can see around six stars with the naked eye, although many more become visible through binoculars or a telescope.
Look towards the east during autumn evenings, where the Pleiades can be found in the constellation Taurus.
Orionid meteor shower
![A green line cuts through a starry sky, capturing a meteor passing through the atmosphere](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/854/cpsprodpb/f917/live/67f7fd60-ad15-11f1-826f-933990eae6f0.jpg)
The Orionid meteor shower observed in the night sky on October 22, 2025 in Dezhou, Shandong Province of China
The Orionid meteor shower is active from early October into November, reaching its peak around 21 October.
Twice each year, Earth passes through trails of dust and debris left behind by Halley's comet. As these tiny particles enter Earth's atmosphere at high speed, they heat up and produce the streaks of light we see as meteors.
The Orionids appear to radiate from the constellation Orion, which gives the shower its name.
For the best chance of seeing them, find somewhere dark and away from artificial lights and allow your eyes time to adjust.
November planetary parade
![In a dark blue, almost black, sky the two planets of Jupiter and Venus shine brightly in the distance.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/820/cpsprodpb/2ca4/live/fc9bc9f0-ad16-11f1-826f-933990eae6f0.jpg)
Jupiter and Venus are two of the planets which will be easy to see in the sky in mid-November
Early risers could be treated to a gathering of Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter around 14 November.
All four planets will be above the horizon before sunrise, although some will be easier to spot than others.
Mercury will be particularly challenging because it remains low in the sky and close to the glare of the rising sun.
Venus and Jupiter, meanwhile, are among the brightest objects in our night sky and should be much easier to pick out.
Leonid meteor shower
![A rocky outcrop and the tops of some trees appear in the bottom left corner underneath a starry, indigo-coloured sky with a meteor streaking across in the top right corner.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/879/cpsprodpb/5329/live/fda702f0-ad17-11f1-826f-933990eae6f0.jpg)
You don't need binoculars or a telescope to see meteors, just give your eyes sometime to adjust to looking up at the night sky
Another meteor shower arrives later in November, with the Leonids expected to peak around 17 November.
The Leonids can travel at about 70km per second as they enter the Earth's atmosphere, making them some of the fastest meteors visible from Earth.
Under ideal, dark sky conditions, around 10 to 15 Leonids an hour can be visible at the shower's peak, although the actual number seen will depend on weather, light pollution and the brightness of the Moon.
They get their name from the constellation Leo, from which the meteors appear to radiate.
The best time to look is generally after midnight and before dawn, when Leo is higher in the sky.
The Beaver supermoon
![A bright full Moon rises above a castle tower made of grey stone with a small peaked roof. There are some layers of cloud in the distance of a dark black sky.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/926/cpsprodpb/759c/live/ed55f590-ad18-11f1-826f-933990eae6f0.jpg)
A November supermoon rising over Bamburgh Castle in Northumberland in 2016
November's full Moon is known as the Beaver Moon. The name is thought to come from the time of year when beavers were particularly active, preparing their lodges and storing food ahead of winter.
It will also be a supermoon, reaching full phase on 24 November.
A supermoon occurs when a full Moon is relatively close to Earth, making it appear slightly larger and brighter.
The November supermoon is also the first of a run of four full Moons which can be classed as supermoons, running through to February 2027.
Be sure to make the most of your autumn skywatching by checking the weather first on the BBC Weather app or online.
summary: Longer autumn nights in the northern hemisphere provide numerous opportunities to observe astronomical events. Upcoming spectacles include the Pleiades star cluster, the Orionid and Leonid meteor showers, a November planetary parade, and a Beaver supermoon. These events offer various stargazing highlights from October through November.
key_points: The Pleiades star cluster, or Seven Sisters, becomes prominent in the eastern autumn sky within the constellation Taurus.
The Orionid meteor shower peaks around October 21 as Earth passes through debris from Halley's comet.
Mercury, Venus, Mars, and Jupiter will gather for a planetary parade visible before sunrise on November 14.
The Leonid meteor shower peaks around November 17, featuring fast-moving meteors traveling at about 70km per second.
November's full Beaver Moon will appear as a supermoon on November 24, appearing slightly larger and brighter due to its proximity to Earth.

title: How to plan and where to go for the "eclipse of the century" – the 2027 total solar eclipse
author: Jamie Carter
content:
![Total solar eclipse, Vicuña, Chile, 2019](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/eucVvN6wZpWBawdkZqqq4F.jpg) 
The total solar eclipse on August 02 2027 will bring 6 minutes and 22 seconds of totality – the longest until 2114 – to Luxor, the temple-strewn capital of ancient Egypt. But while media attention will focus on Luxor and the Nile, photographers actually have thousands of miles of eclipse track to choose from – including many well-known holiday locations.
On August 02, the moon’s shadow will cross southern Spain and Gibraltar before sweeping across North Africa and the Middle East.
With favorable clear-sky prospects across much of the route, maximum duration needn’t be the priority. Solar altitude, landscape, heat, accessibility and mobility could all matter more than another few seconds of totality.
For photographers, there’s only one way to plan an eclipse trip – start with the photograph you want to come home with.
 ![Map showing path of Total solar eclipse on August 2, 2017](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/xB4PwhmPrWAipkujsuVAv4.jpg) 
How to plan for the 2027 total solar eclipse
If you want to photograph the totally-eclipsed sun, there is one non-negotiable rule: you must be inside the path of totality. A 99% partial solar eclipse is not remotely the same thing – and will not give you the full experience or the photographic opportunities.
However, you don’t necessarily need to be precisely on the centerline. Moving toward the edge of the path can cost surprisingly little duration while putting you somewhere with better landscape, clearer weather prospects, or easier road access.
Before booking anything, decide what photograph you want. Use eclipse maps (such as Xavier Jubier’s Interactive Google Map) alongside apps such as The Photographer’s Ephemeris (which has a highly detailed Solar Eclipse Simulator), PhotoPills or PlanItPro to investigate the altitude and azimuth of the sun from potential locations.
The best camera deals, reviews, product advice, and unmissable photography news, direct to your inbox!
Then work backward from your intended foreground. If you want a castle, mountain, mosque or ancient temple beneath the eclipsed sun, where do you actually need to stand? It could be hundreds of meters or even several kilometers away.
Solar altitude matters, especially in 2027. Around the Strait of Gibraltar, the eclipsed sun will be roughly 38° above the southeast horizon. By Luxor, it will be around 82° high – almost overhead.
That’s awkward if you imagined the eclipsed sun hanging above an Egyptian temple. It’s also awkward for telephoto images of the corona, because it means cameras will need to point almost vertically upward in temperatures exceeding 104°F / 40°C.
Make sure your tripod head can support a long lens at a steep angle, shade equipment before totality, keep spare batteries cool, and watch for overheating warnings, particularly when shooting video.
Above all, scout your composition, not just your location. If possible, arrive a few days early and visit prospective sites at approximately the same time of day as totality.
Where to photograph the 2027 total solar eclipse: Spain
 ![Tarifa,Andalusia, Spain. Photo taken on the 28th of May 2025.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/jGoHbKCr2w6L9M6uBiGwac.jpg) 
For European photographers, southern Spain is the easy option. Totality is shorter than in North Africa, but the sun is lower and in the southeast, making it easier to combine with beaches, mountains, villages and the ocean. Infrastructure, road access and the ability to drive in with your own equipment are other major advantages.
Málaga (1 min 54 secs). 
Totality is relatively short, but excellent transport links, plentiful accommodation and a long Mediterranean waterfront make this one of the easiest places from which to photograph the eclipse.
Cádiz (2 mins 56 secs). 
One of Europe’s oldest cities sits on a narrow peninsula almost surrounded by the Atlantic, with its historic skyline, waterfront and beaches offering plenty of potential foregrounds.
Tarifa (4 mins 40 secs). 
Close to the centerline and overlooking the Strait of Gibraltar towards Morocco, Tarifa combines a long totality with beaches, mountains and seascapes.
Where to photograph the 2027 total solar eclipse: Morocco
 ![Chefchaouen, Morocco](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/KDhBZBBFquyWcVk3HXqYkR.jpg) 
Morocco combines almost five minutes of totality with a relatively low sun, making its coastlines, medinas and Rif Mountains particularly attractive for environmental eclipse photography.
Tangier (4 mins 50 secs). 
A historic port overlooking the Strait of Gibraltar, with the medina, coastline and views towards Spain.
Tétouan (4 mins 51 secs). 
Its UNESCO-listed medina, whitewashed architecture and proximity to the Rif Mountains offer plenty of possibilities for combining totality with a distinctive Moroccan foreground.
Chefchaouen (3 mins 39 secs). 
You sacrifice more than a minute compared with Tangier, but the famous blue-painted city and dramatic Rif Mountains could make that an attractive trade for photographers.
Where to photograph the 2027 total solar eclipse: Algeria
 ![Oran, Algeria](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/f7MN3vMvZf5LthiEWp37R5.jpg) 
Algeria could suit photographers looking for landscapes and locations far removed from the major eclipse-tour circuits. Oran is the obvious starting point because it is a major coastal city with ferry links to Spain, while locations farther inland are closer to the centerline.
Oran (5 mins 9 secs). 
Algeria’s second-largest city sits on the Mediterranean coast and offers a relatively practical base, with coastal scenery, Santa Cruz fort above, and more than five minutes of totality.
Mostaganem (5 mins 7 secs). 
Farther east along the Mediterranean coast, this less-visited city combines a long totality with beaches, cliffs and coastal landscapes.
M’Sila (5 mins 22 secs). 
Head inland for a longer eclipse, increasingly arid scenery and excellent prospects for clear skies — an interesting option for photographers prioritizing the eclipse over tourism infrastructure.
Where to photograph the 2027 total solar eclipse: Tunisia
 ![Mos Espa, located in the Tunisian Sahara near Tozeur and Nefta, is an abandoned film set from the Star Wars franchise. This fictional city, nestled between two salt lakes, Chott El Djerid and Chott El Gharsa, served as a remote spaceport in the galaxy.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/dpimDxv4Hpod99cUhLXjka.jpg) 
Tunisia offers a choice between Star Wars desert landscapes near the southern edge of the path and much longer totality around Sfax on the Mediterranean coast.
Tozeur (1 min 43 secs). 
Totality is relatively brief, but the surrounding desert contains some of Tunisia’s most famous Star Wars locations, including the nearby Mos Espa sets.
Sidi Bouhlel (3 mins 9 secs). 
Better known to movie fans as “Star Wars Canyon,” its rugged desert landscape could provide one of the most distinctive eclipse foregrounds anywhere along the path.
Sfax (5 mins 41 secs). 
Tunisia’s second-largest city combines almost six minutes of totality with a Mediterranean location, good infrastructure and excellent prospects for clear skies.
Where to photograph the 2027 total solar eclipse: Egypt
 ![Colossi of Memnon at dawn with hot air balloons in the sky, Luxor, Nile Valley, Egypt](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/JnJuMYehD6jWeQhSCBzQNQ.jpg) 
For sheer spectacle — as well as bragging rights — Egypt will be impossible to beat. The path crosses the Nile Valley near Luxor, where totality lasts about 6 mins 22 secs beneath some of the most reliable clear skies on the eclipse track. Dust, extreme heat and a throng of humanity may be bigger concerns than clouds.
Six minutes of totality is an extraordinary luxury. There will still be the usual scramble around the diamond rings and Baily’s beads, but plenty of time between them to photograph the corona, stop shooting and simply look up.
However, Luxor may not be the best place in Egypt for photographers. It will be exceptionally busy — accommodation is already in incredibly high demand and access to sites such as Karnak and the Valley of the Kings will likely be restricted. Don’t plan your photography around setting up a tripod inside a famous archaeological site.
Many visitors will watch from Nile cruise boats, but a moving, vibrating platform isn’t ideal for long-lens photography. Nearby boats could also mean engines, music, announcements and artificial lights during totality.
The path covers a long stretch of the Nile Valley, so consider looking beyond Luxor. Esna and Edfu have major temples and lie inside the path, while Kom Ombo is closer to its southern edge. All could be quieter alternatives, although transport and access will require careful planning.
Another catch awaits anyone dreaming of the eclipsed sun hanging above an Egyptian temple. Around Luxor, the sun will be about 82 degrees high, almost overhead. A conventional telephoto composition of temple-plus-eclipse is therefore unlikely — you may need to move a considerable distance from the monument or use an extremely wide lens to include both.
Alternatively, Egypt could be perfect for a 360-degree camera. Put one on a tripod, start recording before totality and leave it alone. It can capture the approaching shadow, changing landscape, sunset-like horizon and reactions around you, and you can reframe the footage afterward. Best of all, there’s nothing to operate during totality.
Luxor (6 mins 22 secs). 
The headline destination, with maximum-duration totality, exceptionally favorable clear-sky prospects and some of the world’s most famous ancient monuments — but expect huge crowds.
Siwa Oasis (5 mins 31 secs). 
Deep in Egypt’s Western Desert near the Libyan border, Siwa offers palm groves, salt lakes, dunes and desert landscapes beneath more than five minutes of totality — a compelling alternative to the crowds of the Nile Valley.
Edfu (about 5 mins 40 secs). 
South of Luxor and home to the remarkably well-preserved Temple of Horus, Edfu combines a long totality with an extraordinary ancient Egyptian setting.
Plan to experience the eclipse
 ![Temple of Kom Ombo. Sunset landscape with ancient building architecture near Nile river, Egypt.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ioq7jfpLf4rQGihWQXoN55.jpg) 
A total solar eclipse is one of photography’s most alluring subjects because the most memorable image may not be the technically perfect close-up of the corona. It could be a wide-angle frame showing the landscape plunged into twilight, a photograph of someone’s reaction, a 360-degree recording of the moon’s shadow arriving, or a creative composition yet to be dreamed up.
Whatever destination you choose, arrive with a plan – and preferably a simple one. Know exactly where the sun will be, scout your location, endlessly rehearse your equipment, and automate as much as you can. Always have a Plan B in case of cloud.
Plan the photographs now, then book your flights and accommodation as soon as possible. But the priority always has to be the same – when the moon’s shadow arrives on August 2, 2027, you should spend as little time as possible operating cameras and as much as possible looking up. However, with such a long totality to play with this time, savvy eclipse photographers could be in for the eclipse of a lifetime.
YOU MIGHT ALSO LIKE…
If you're photographing the eclipse, make sure you're using the best solar filters for your camera. For astro shooting, check out the best cameras for astrophotography, the best lenses for astrophotography and the best star tracker camera mounts.
![Jamie Carter](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/SR4bDfnvXXTBQxDYnYM2bb.jpg) 
Jamie has been writing about photography, astronomy, astro-tourism and astrophotography for over 20 years, producing content for Forbes.com, Space.com, Live Science, Techradar, T3, BBC Wildlife, Science Focus, New Scientist, Sky & Telescope, BBC Sky At Night, South China Morning Post, The Guardian, The Telegraph and Travel+Leisure.
As the editor of When Is The Next Eclipse and author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, he has a wealth of experience, expertise and enthusiasm for astrophotography, from capturing the Northern Lights, the moon and meteor showers to solar and lunar eclipses.
He also brings a great deal of knowledge on action cameras, 360 cameras, AI cameras, camera backpacks, telescopes, gimbals, tripods and all manner of photography equipment.
