summary: The total solar eclipse on August 2, 2027, will offer up to 6 minutes and 22 seconds of totality across southern Spain, North Africa, and the Middle East. Photographers must plan their compositions carefully by considering the sun's high altitude, local weather, and potential crowds, especially in headline destinations like Luxor, Egypt. By evaluating alternative locations in countries like Spain, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Egypt, travelers can secure unique foregrounds and better viewing conditions.
key_points: The August 2, 2027 total solar eclipse will feature an exceptionally long duration of totality, reaching up to 6 minutes and 22 seconds in Luxor, Egypt.
Photographers need to be strictly inside the path of totality and should choose locations based on desired foregrounds, accessibility, and solar altitude.
Solar altitude varies significantly along the route, with the sun sitting at roughly 38 degrees in Gibraltar and nearly 82 degrees overhead in Luxor.
Recommended viewing regions include southern Spain, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Egypt, each offering distinct landscapes ranging from Mediterranean coasts to desert ruins.
Experts advise scouting locations early, preparing equipment for extreme heat, and balancing camera operation with actually experiencing the eclipse.

title: Black Holes or Black Hole Stars? Astronomers Spar Over Webb Telescope’s ‘Little Red Dots.’ | Quanta Magazine
author: Charlie Wood September
content:
![](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Black-Hole-Star-cr-Mark-Belan-Lede-1.webp) 
Mark Belan/Quanta Magazine
Introduction
Astronomers built the James Webb Space Telescope to pick up faint light from the first billion years after the Big Bang, a chaotic era when vast swaths of hydrogen and helium gas gathered into the chains of galaxies we see today. Even in the telescope’s first images, astronomers could see a whole zoo of mysterious smears of light.
One batch of objects proved especially difficult to interpret. They glowed blindingly bright, emitting red light with long wavelengths and shining as brilliantly as a whole galaxy. They were tiny, spanning just a pixel. And they were everywhere. A couple appear in almost every image Webb takes. In 2023, researchers started calling them “little red dots.” Astronomers have repeatedly pointed Webb toward the little red dots, wringing precious new information from these pixels of light.
Initially, researchers thought the dots looked kind of like galaxies. Later, they concluded that little red dots look more like the supermassive black holes that sit at the heart of most galaxies. These monstrous masses are themselves dark, but their formidable gravity violently vacuums up gas and other nearby matter, generating rings of hot, swirling detritus that completely outshine the stars around them.
Then, in the spring of 2025, two teams of astronomers simultaneously announced observations of a pair of little red dots that were unlike all the rest. In fact, they were unlike any object ever seen.
“In all the millions of [observations] we’ve taken with ground-based telescopes,” said Anna de Graaff, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy in Heidelberg, Germany, and head of one group, “there’s nothing that looks like these sources.”
The two teams of astronomers propose that they are looking at a new astronomical object: a topsy-turvy lump of hydrogen that shines with the light of billions of suns while hiding a black hole deep in its core. They call it a black hole star.
![A woman stands in the midst of small red circles mounted on poles.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ANNA_DE_GRAAFF©maxborchardt-2156.webp) 
Anna de Graaff of the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy in Heidelberg, Germany, suspects that many of the little red dots are giant stars with black holes hidden inside them.
Max Borchardt
In a paper posted last week, astronomers took this analysis a step further. They argued that the Webb telescope is witnessing the births of supermassive black holes inside the cores of colossal stars. “There is a fundamentally new phenomenon afoot,” said Rohan Naidu, an astronomer at the University of Hawai‘i.
But not everyone agrees with this bold interpretation. It has sparked a flurry of follow-up research and reignited a fierce debate over the nature of these peculiar pinpricks of light.
“The field has gotten very polarized,” said Anna-Christina Eilers, an astrophysicist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who studies little red dots.
The Mystery of the Little Red Dots
When all you can see is a speck, it’s hard to tell what you’re looking at. All you know about it is its color and brightness. Astronomers first argued that little red dots were distant galaxies on the cosmic horizon, mainly because of their brightness. But galaxies that bright would have to be huge — and there was no known way for them to grow so big in just hundreds of millions of years. Astronomers dubbed them “universe breakers” for the way they seemed to demolish the standard cosmic timeline.
Then they took a closer look. De Graaff led one survey, called Red Unknowns: Bright Infrared Extragalactic Survey (Rubies), and Naidu co-led another survey, called Mirage or Miracle (MOM). These were two of a wave of surveys that trained Webb telescope on distant objects, including little red dots, for hours at a time. They tabulated precisely what shades of light were coming from each dot, and how bright the shades were. This detailed color breakdown, known as a spectrum, told astronomers a far more detailed story than the initial observations had. Different atoms shine in subtly different hues, so the spectrum provided a sense of what the object’s particles were doing.
The bombshell discovery in the little red dot spectra was that the colors of hydrogen were smeared out across multiple shades. Usually, seeing such an effect means you’re looking straight at an exposed black hole. Black holes whip hydrogen clouds around them at furious rates, with the clouds emitting slightly different colors depending on their speed. The net effect is that instead of seeing just the hue of hydrogen, you see a range of colors called a broad line. The wider this range, the faster the fastest hydrogen clouds are flying — and the more massive the black hole.
Many astronomers concluded that big black holes dotted the universe, washing out the light of the stars in their host galaxies. As black holes, the little red dots would appear red because dust — grainy stuff much more complicated than gas — was blocking their blue light.
Yet they still seemed weird. Most supermassive black holes flicker as they gulp down chunky streams of gas around them. They also beam powerful X-rays across the universe. Most little red dots seemed to be doing neither of these things.
But that didn’t trouble astronomers much; they expected to see some strangeness during the pandemonium of the early universe. And at least the black holes weren’t breaking any cosmological theories.
Then, in the spring of 2025, de Graaff and Naidu’s teams unveiled the two strangest dots yet.
A New Interpretation
What made these two little red dots exceptional was how red they were. Webb picked up almost no light in the bluer hues of their spectra. And at a particular shade of red, the colors abruptly got much, much brighter. This feature, known as a Balmer break, is something you see when looking at a hot ball of hydrogen gas — typically, certain types of stars or galaxies (which are made of many stars). Deep in a star’s core, nuclear fusion pumps out heat and light, which slowly filters up to the star’s surface. There, hydrogen atoms can become energized in a way that blocks bluer light and lets through only redder light. These red colors have a hump-shaped spectrum that reveals the overall temperature of the star’s surface.
But the new little red dots couldn’t literally be stars — they were way too bright. And they didn’t look much like black holes either. Black holes have an assortment of ringlike structures of different temperatures. They don’t typically produce a Balmer break, or the red, hump-shaped curve indicative of a stellar surface burning at a uniform 5,000 or so degrees Kelvin.
Naidu and de Graaff concluded that they were looking at the first examples of something combining the vigor of a black hole with the outward appearance of a star: a black hole star.
From the outside, a black hole star would appear as a huge agglomeration of hydrogen gas. If our sun were replaced with a black hole star, it would extend a dozen times farther than the orbit of Pluto. Out toward the edge, the star would boil unstably, sloughing off outer layers and explosively ejecting mass. “It’s going to be a very messy system where stuff is being blown out and falling back in,” de Graaff said. “I wouldn’t want to come too close.”
Deep in the center, invisible to the outside world, the star would be powered by a black hole. This black hole would pull gas around it, dramatically heating it and pushing light and energy outward, which would keep the outer layers of hydrogen from collapsing inward. In this way, the black hole would form the “engine” of the star, analogous to the fusion-powered core of our sun. Moving outward, material swirling around the black hole would beam out a range of colors that would slowly make their way toward the surface. And as with certain stars, the hydrogen near the surface would stop the bluer light while letting the redder light pass through. The end result would be a gassy surface shining as brightly as a more exposed black hole but with the Balmer break and smooth red hump of a 5,000-kelvin star, de Graaff and Naidu theorized. As a bonus, the gas “cocoon” would also block X-rays, and the gas wouldn’t flicker much — which would explain two mysteries surrounding other little red dots.
But what about the broad lines, supposedly caused by hydrogen swirling fast around a black hole? Another group provided a possible explanation.
The group, which included Vadim Rusakov, an astronomer at the University of Manchester, had been scrutinizing the broad lines of the best-observed little red dots. Broad lines take the shape of a sharp mountain peak. But Rusakov and collaborators noticed that in many cases, these mountains sloped slightly more gently than would be expected if they came from fast-moving gas around a black hole. So they suggested that instead of coming from rotating gas, much of the spread of the hydrogen colors could come from light scattering off electrons.
They digitally removed the effect of this electron-induced smudging from their data, Rusakov said. After that, the broad lines stopped looking quite so broad and started looking more like light passing through a sluggishly churning shell of hydrogen gas in a particular state, similar to what you’d expect to see from a black hole star. The three teams — de Graaff’s, Naidu’s, and Rusakov’s — posted their findings on March 20, 2025 — “black hole star date,” as some of the researchers called it.
Black hole stars could represent a new stage in the development of a supermassive black hole: First, a black hole would form in the center of a shell of hydrogen, together with a baby galaxy of normal stars around it. Then, over time, the black hole would eat its way out of its cocoon, gaining mass as it cleared the hydrogen gas away.
“We are seeing the seed,” Naidu said. “This is the birth of potentially every massive black hole in the universe.”
The Argument Against
The black hole star enthusiasts appeal to Occam’s razor, arguing that their theory gives the simplest accounting of these two little red dots, and perhaps of little red dots in general. But simple is subjective, and astronomers have spent the last year in a lively debate about what’s really going on.
Even years after the discovery of the first little red dot, not much about them is settled. Dale Kocevski, an astrophysicist at Colby College, recalls leading a discussion about them at an April 2026 conference in Aspen, Colorado. He started by recapping what he hoped would be an uncontroversial idea about their trace amounts of blue light. “The group erupted into argument, and we couldn’t even get past the first bullet point,” he said.
Many astronomers still argue that little red dots are traditional black holes — even the new duo. “The data is really compelling,” said Roberto Maiolino of the University of Cambridge. “I’m a little bit more dubious about the interpretation.”
For each point in favor of black hole stars, Maiolino fires off a quick rebuttal. The lack of flicker? In the early universe, black holes may have had a steadier food supply and may therefore have been tidier eaters. The lack of X-rays? Standard galactic black holes are ringed by a thick doughnut of gas and dust, which can block most X-rays. He sees no reason to suspect the little red dots of being anything other than standard supermassive black holes.
The redness of the new objects is striking, he said, and he agrees that it means there must be a ton of gas between the black hole and us. But that gas could come in the form of the doughnut, or as puffy clouds that fill in patches of the black hole’s sky, as opposed to the shell of gas around a black hole star. Maiolino agrees that electron scattering likely contributes to broadening the lines in the spectra of some of the little red dots. But electron scattering also smears hydrogen lines from supermassive black holes, he said.
Maiolino and his collaborator, Piero Madau of the University of California, Santa Cruz, argue that the redness of the dots comes mainly from the angle at which we see them. The reddest dots are those that we happen to see edge on, their gassy doughnuts blocking our view. Webb also sees some “little blue dots.” These could be the same exposed black holes, viewed top-down, Maiolino and Madau pointed out in spring 2026. They also appeal to Occam’s razor — in this case arguing that black holes are a simpler explanation for little dots of all colors.
At this stage either theory — black hole or black hole star — could match what Webb telescope has seen. “I don’t think that there is a compelling reason to prefer one or the other,” said Mauro Giavalisco, an astronomer at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst who has spent much of his career interpreting the spectra of distant galaxies.
To test their interpretations, astronomers need a clearer picture of how black hole stars might form and how exactly they expect them to look.
Return of the Quasi-Star
Over the last few years, Mitchell Begelman has been teaching a graduate student seminar on little red dots at the University of Colorado, Boulder. It’s kept him reading the firehose of papers coming out on the subject. In these mysterious objects that weren’t quite stars and weren’t quite black holes, he recognized a ghost from his past: the quasi-star. “Suddenly the switch flipped, and I realized that this is what quasi-stars should look like,” Begelman said.
Begelman had proposed the existence of quasi-stars back in 2006, along with Marta Volonteri and Martin Rees, to explain observations of what looked like impossibly massive black holes.
Their quasi-star theory offers one way to make a black hole star: The core of a vast gas cloud collapses to directly form a black hole, gathering the remainder of the cloud around it.
In 2025, Begelman and his collaborator Jason Dexter applied the quasi-star model to the little red dots. They estimated that quasi-stars could quickly assemble themselves in a few million years before settling into a more mature form that would look just like little red dots. They would do this for tens of millions of years — lasting long enough for Webb to spot them.
In 2026, Giavalisco worked with a team to flesh out the quasi-star model as an origin for black hole stars, which he finds to be a natural way of explaining how little red dots could mask the signs of a feeding black hole. He points out that our sun performs the same trick, hiding its explosive fusion, just on a much smaller scale. “We have billions and billions of hydrogen bombs exploding every second, and yet we see none of them,” he said.
Giavalisco and his collaborators found that their new model of a quasi-star fit the spectra of de Graaf’s and Naidu’s objects even better than the initial models had. He thinks the quasi-star theory is a plausible explanation for the little red dots but remains open to other ideas. “I just want to know the truth,” he said.
In the meantime, researchers are starting to search for another distinguishing pattern: If little red dots are black hole stars formed in the early universe, then they should grow rarer over time as they each break free from their shells and reveal their inner black holes.
In an August 2026 census of both red and blue dots broken up into different eras, Kocevski of Colby College and his collaborators found exactly that pattern. In the data, as the universe approaches 2 billion to 3 billion years of age, the little red dots seem to vanish — preliminary evidence that little red dots, as black hole stars, might really be a puberty-like phase for many supermassive black holes.
Theorists are already working out what that puberty-like phase might be like. In another analysis, posted on September 8, Naidu, de Graaff, Eilers, and their collaborators tested out an assortment of techniques for deducing the mass of a black hole “seed” inside a black hole star. These hidden black holes seemed to be far less massive than standard, exposed black holes. The scientists propose that Webb is catching supermassive black hole stars — up to 1 million times the mass of the sun — in the act of incubating the universe’s first big black holes.
Some researchers, including Kocevski, still aren’t sure. Kocevski suspects that the universe is a messy place, and that some little red dots are truly as starlike as the black hole star camp is arguing. Others, he thinks, will be more like standard black holes, as the other camp argues. “I have a sneaking suspicion that we’re both right,” he said.

![](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/HilbertSpace-cr-Tommy-Parket-Default.webp) 
![Close-up view of a chandelier-like dilution refrigerator used in quantum computing, with many gold-colored wires hanging between levels of gold plates.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2056/08/IBMs-quantum-computer-cr-Graham-Carlow-Default.webp)
summary: Since the James Webb Space Telescope began operations, astronomers have observed numerous bright, tiny objects in the early universe known as "little red dots." While initially mistaken for distant galaxies, they were later largely interpreted as supermassive black holes obscured by dust. Recently, some researchers analyzed new data and proposed that these dots may represent a previously unknown phenomenon called "black hole stars"—gigantic spheres of hydrogen gas with black holes hidden at their cores. However, this bold hypothesis remains deeply controversial, with other astronomers arguing that standard supermassive black hole models can still explain the observations.
key_points: The James Webb Space Telescope discovered numerous mysterious, bright, and tiny objects in the early universe dubbed "little red dots."
Researchers initially debated whether the dots were distant galaxies or supermassive black holes, eventually favoring obscured black holes.
In early 2025, two research teams proposed a new explanation for exceptionally red dots: "black hole stars," which combine a hydrogen star's exterior appearance with a black hole core.
Proponents argue that black hole stars could explain why the objects lack typical black hole flickering and X-ray emissions while displaying stellar-like spectral features.
Many astronomers remain skeptical of the black hole star theory, arguing that traditional models involving standard supermassive black holes surrounded by gas and dust can still account for the data.

title: Here's how to catch up on sleep, the right way
author: Amanda Ruggeri
content:
Here's how to catch up on sleep, the right way
![BBC Serenity Strull/ Getty Images A woman asleep on a giant pillow, surrounded by a blue night sky (Credit: BBC/ Serenity Strull/ Getty Images)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p94bgb.jpg.webp) BBC Serenity Strull/ Getty Images
Just two hours of extra sleep can help reverse the damage from a bad night. But early nights and lie-ins should be wielded with caution.
We've all been there: waking up, bleary-eyed after a bad night, feeling exhausted. "It's fine," we tell ourselves. "I'll catch up at the weekend."
For some of us, this experience is a one-off. For others, it's a way of life. One survey of nearly 8,000 US adults found that nearly half regularly slept in on the weekends. Perhaps unsurprisingly, teenagers seem to have the biggest weekend lie-ins of any age group.
A bit of extra sleep can be especially tempting for those of us who don't get enough during the week. Adults are generally advised to aim for around seven to nine hours, while it's thought that most adolescents need between eight and ten. But that's not always possible.
Which leads to the million-dollar question: if you aren't sleeping enough during the week, should you sleep in on the weekend? And if you do, can this blunt the effects of short sleep?
The risk of a lie-in
To understand why sleeping in might have downsides, it helps to look at the two main processes regulating sleep.
The first, the sleep homeostat, is like a "sleep tank". The longer we're awake, the more it fills with sleep pressure – and the more we feel like we need to lie down and snooze. The second, our circadian rhythm, gets adjusted every day by our exposure to light and dark, temperature changes, even when we eat or move. These work together to make us feel sleepy, ideally at an appropriate time each night. (Learn more about how regulating your rhythm can aid your sleep in my newsletter course, How to Sleep Better, launching on 21 September 2026.)
Catching up on sleep can knock both our sleep homeostat and our body clock off. This is true whether you go to bed earlier, or sleep in. Because extra morning sleep reduces our sleep pressure later in the day, we might not feel tired until later that evening. And because we're not just sleeping at a different time, but doing everything else at a different time – including getting light exposure – it can affect our circadian rhythm too.
The result? We might sleep in Sunday morning and fall asleep later on Sunday night, so that when our alarm goes off at 06:00 on Monday, we haven't slept enough – starting the cycle all over again. "It's like shifting time zones every single week," says Melynda Casement, sleep psychologist and director of the University of Oregon Sleep Lab.
However, though catch-up sleep should be used cautiously, it's not always a bad idea. Here's when it might be helpful to get some extra rest.
The benefits of recovery sleep
How short sleep impacts our health and cognition is still being untangled. But in carefully controlled sleep restriction experiments, it's become clear that an especially rough night impacts our physiology. And at least some of these consequences can be blunted, if not reversed, with catch-up sleep.
In one study, for example, people who got only two hours' sleep for a single night showed higher counts of two types of white blood cells, potentially indicating a physiological stress response. Some participants were then granted an eight-hour sleep the following night. But even after this, their white blood cell counts hadn't fully bounced back. However, participants who were allowed to sleep for up to 10 hours on the second day had levels which had nearly returned back to the baseline.
![BBC/ Serenity Strull/ Getty Images Catching up on sleep can help to reverse some of the physiological damage caused by a bad night (Credit: BBC/ Serenity Strull/ Getty Images)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p94bl0.jpg.webp) BBC/ Serenity Strull/ Getty Images
Another experiment studied what happened when 11 men who normally slept for eight hours each night were limited to four. Six nights of short sleep were enough to impair their glucose clearance and insulin responses. If sustained long-term, these physiological changes can raise the risk of type two diabetes. But after six more nights of a 12-hour sleep opportunity, their measures had returned to baseline levels.
None of that means that a weekend lie-in (or early night) counteracts every effect of sleep debt, especially when short sleep persists over weeks or months. Vigilant attention (our ability to stay focused and respond quickly) and spatial orientation seem to be particularly vulnerable. In these cases, even weekend catch-up sleep can't fully reverse the effects of short weekday sleep.
Then there's also naps. These can also be beneficial for people running short. But they're usually studied separately from overnight catch-up sleep. (Read more from the BBC about why power naps might be good for our health.)
Catching up on sleep, saving lives
But these studies were conducted in artificial laboratory conditions. What happens when people catch up on sleep in the real world?
For one Swedish study, researchers followed more than 40,000 adults over 13 years. They found that adults under 65 years old who regularly slept for six to seven hours a night had the lowest risk of death. In comparison, those who slept five hours or less had a 65% greater mortality risk. For adults over 65, there was no association between short sleep and mortality risk – a result, the researchers suggest, of our sleep needs decreasing as we age.
But there was a twist. A decent weekend sleep appeared to erase the additional risk for the five-hour-or-less sleepers. If the short sleepers caught up then, statistically they had no higher risk of death than the people who slept a healthy amount during the week.
Even when short sleep's health impacts aren't reversed by catch-up sleep, they're often ameliorated. One study of almost 2,800 Korean adults, for example, found that habitually short sleepers were about 73% more likely to have high blood pressure. But each hour of weekend catch-up sleep was linked to about 17% less risk.
Other studies have found that short weekday sleepers who sleep in on weekends have a lower risk of dementia. They also have decreased risk of metabolic syndrome, a cluster of symptoms that raise your risk of type 2 diabetes or cardiovascular disease.
More like this:
Not all studies have found a benefit of weekend catch-up sleep. One large UK-based study found no link between catch-up sleep and mortality or cardiovascular disease. But it didn't find a greater risk of sleeping in, either.
Put together, these findings help explain why some scientists argue that waking up at the same time every day, no matter what, may backfire.
"Some people even go so far as saying, put on your alarm clock, even on weekends, so that you're regular," says Till Roenneberg, professor emeritus of chronobiology at LMU Munich's Institute for Medical Psychology, Germany. He disagrees. "Of course you have to catch up on sleep," he says. "Sleep is one of the most important functions in our lives."
The exception is people who have insomnia. The usual treatment for this condition recommends that people avoid both earlier bedtimes and lie-ins. This is true even after a rough night, as it can throw off their rhythms and make sleep even harder to attain.
A realistic sweet spot
The next question is how much catch-up sleep you should have to maximise the benefits and minimise the downsides.
Studies in the US and Korea have found this amount is associated with the lowest risk of depression. It's also been linked to lower inflammation in adults who are habitual short sleepers. Researchers have found a similar pattern for younger people, including a lower risk of anxiety and depression.
So, a little lie-in can sometimes be a good idea. But it probably won’t justify waking up at lunchtime.
* Amanda Ruggeri is a journalist who explores the science, psychology and history of the ideas we take for granted. She writes the six-part How to Sleep Better newsletter course, and her upcoming book, The Sleep Myth, will be published in summer 2027.
* All content within this article is provided for general information only, and should not be treated as a substitute for the medical advice of health care professionals.
--
summary: Catching up on sleep after a bad night or a week of short sleep can help reverse physiological damage and lower health risks such as high blood pressure and mortality. However, excessive or careless lie-ins and early nights can disrupt the sleep homeostat and circadian rhythm, essentially feeling like shifting time zones every week. While beneficial for many, recovery sleep should be used cautiously, and individuals with insomnia should avoid altering their schedules with lie-ins.
key_points: Just two hours of extra sleep can help reverse the physiological damage caused by a bad night, such as elevated stress markers.
Weekend lie-ins or early nights can disrupt both the sleep homeostat and the circadian rhythm, potentially making it harder to sleep on Sunday night.
Studies suggest that regular weekend catch-up sleep can help lower the risk of mortality, high blood pressure, and metabolic issues for habitual short sleepers.
Recovery sleep cannot fully reverse all effects of long-term sleep deprivation, particularly regarding vigilant attention and spatial orientation.
People with insomnia are advised to avoid lie-ins and earlier bedtimes because it can throw off their sleep rhythms.

title: Indoor vs outdoor cycling: Which exercise is best for fitness, strength and bone health
author: Hannah Bradfield
content:
Cycling is having a huge moment right now, with more people than ever taking to the saddle to improve their health and fitness.
According to a Transport for London report published last year, cycling journeys in the capital alone increased by 43% over six years, reaching 1.5 million a day. Meanwhile, spin has long been one of the world's most popular gym classes.
But when it comes to the specific health benefits, how do indoor and outdoor cycling actually compare?
We asked a sport and exercise medicine doctor to explain the differences.
Indoor vs outdoor cycling: which is better for fitness?
'Neither is objectively better because they train slightly different things,' says Dr David Porter of Opus Biological.
Ultimately, the better option depends on your goal.
'Both build cardiovascular fitness, but outdoor cycling recruits more of the stabilising muscles around the hips, core and shoulders because you're constantly correcting balance, reading the road and adjusting to the terrain,' he explains.
That aligns with the research. A systematic review published in the Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports found clear links between outdoor cycling and improved cardiorespiratory fitness, particularly among younger people. Commuter cycling was also associated with lower all-cause and cancer mortality in middle-aged and older adults.
Indoor cycling performs well too. A separate systematic review published in Medicina highlighted its potential to improve aerobic capacity – one of the key markers of cardiovascular fitness.
The two differ slightly when it comes to strength.
Outdoor riding recruits more stabilising muscles, making it a better option if your goal is broader functional fitness.
Indoor cycling, meanwhile, 'isolates the leg muscles more cleanly, which is genuinely useful if the goal is a structured power or interval session,' says Dr Porter.
Indoor vs outdoor cycling: which is better for recovery and bone health?
'Indoor cycling on a stationary bike or in a studio class is a controlled, low-impact movement pattern: no potholes, no sudden braking, no camber in the road,' says Dr Porter.
'That makes it a good option for anyone building back up after a knee, hip or lower-back injury, or managing early-stage joint issues because the resistance and cadence are fixed and predictable.'
Outdoor cycling, by comparison, exposes you to constantly changing terrain.
'Outdoor riding adds unpredictable terrain and constant small stabilising adjustments, which is harder on the joints in the short term but does more for functional strength and proprioception over time,' he explains.
When it comes to bone health, neither is a complete solution.
'Weight-bearing, impact-loaded activity is what stimulates bone density, and outdoor cycling – particularly on rougher surfaces – provides more of that mechanical loading than a stationary bike,' says Dr Porter.
'It's not a reason to avoid indoor cycling, but anyone using it as their only form of exercise should pair it with some impact or resistance training.'
Supporting that, one study published in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research found that combining indoor cycling with resistance training for nine weeks increased sedentary women's leg strength by almost 30%. Core, back and arm strength also improved, while estimated VO2 max increased by 8.5%.
Should you cycle indoors or outdoors?
'Indoor is the better choice during injury rehab, in poor weather, or for anyone who wants a precise, time-efficient workout with no traffic or navigation to think about,' says Dr Porter.
'Outdoor is better for building genuine bike-handling skills, enjoying the mental health benefits of being outside and preparing for an event that will actually take place on the road.'
That mental health element shouldn't be overlooked.
According to research from the Eden Project, more than half of UK adults (52%) spend less than two hours a week in nature, despite 86% saying it benefits their wellbeing.
So, if it's practical and safe for you to do so, outdoor cycling offers the dual benefit of improving your fitness while spending more time outside.
'Indoor gives you control and consistency, outdoor gives you resilience and skill. Most people would benefit from doing both rather than treating it as a choice between the two,' concludes Dr Porter.
As with any form of exercise, though, the best option is the one you'll actually keep doing.
One of our most frequently asked questions here at Women’s Health? How to build muscle and burn fat at the same time. So, we asked superstar trainer Oyinda Okunowo exactly how to do it. In this 4-week plan – created exclusively for Women’s Health COLLECTIVE members – you’ll get the workouts and nutrition guidance needed to help you on your way to better body composition. Tap the link below to unlock 14 days of free access to Oyinda's plan and start training today.
Hannah Bradfield is a Senior Health and Fitness Writer for Women’s Health UK. An NCTJ-accredited journalist, Hannah graduated from Loughborough University with a BA in English and Sport Science and an MA in Media and Cultural Analysis. She has been covering sports, health and fitness for the last five years and has created content for outlets including BBC Sport, BBC Sounds, Runner’s World and Stylist. She especially enjoys interviewing those working within the community to improve access to sport, exercise and wellness. Hannah is a 2024 John Schofield Trust Fellow and was also named a 2022 Rising Star in Journalism by The Printing Charity. A keen runner, Hannah was firmly a sprinter growing up (also dabbling in long jump) but has since transitioned to longer-distance running. While 10K is her favoured race distance, she loves running or volunteering at parkrun every Saturday, followed, of course, by pastries. She’s always looking for fun new runs and races to do and brunch spots to try.
summary: Both indoor and outdoor cycling build cardiovascular fitness, but they train the body differently depending on your goals and needs. Outdoor cycling engages more stabilising muscles, provides unpredictable terrain, and offers better mechanical loading for bone health and mental wellbeing. Meanwhile, indoor cycling offers controlled, low-impact movements that are ideal for injury rehabilitation, weather disruptions, and structured power training.
key_points: Outdoor cycling recruits more stabilising muscles in the hips, core, and shoulders due to changing terrain and balance adjustments.
Indoor cycling isolates leg muscles more cleanly, making it better for structured power intervals and controlled injury rehabilitation.
Outdoor cycling provides more mechanical loading and rougher surfaces, which do more to stimulate bone density than a stationary bike.
Indoor cycling is ideal for poor weather, time-efficient workouts, and avoiding traffic, while outdoor cycling offers mental health benefits from nature.

title: James Webb Space Telescope discovers the rings of tiny solar system body Chariklo are changing
author: Robert Lea
content:
![(Main) Illustration of the small solar system body Chariklo (Inset) artist's impression of the JWST](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/NqJMLcyVWT96TRxRM8MenY.png) 
Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have discovered that the ring system of a tiny solar system body is even more interesting than they knew.
The object in question is Chariklo, which orbits the sun between Saturn and Uranus, at around 17 times the distance between Earth and the sun. Despite only being around 155 miles (250 kilometers) wide, Chariklo, part of the Centaur family of asteroids, possesses two thick rings. 
Though Saturn is the solar system body most famous for its rings, other planets also have ring systems, albeit less prominent. That includes Uranus, Neptune, and Jupiter. However, Chariklo and the even smaller body Chiron, show that even the most diminutive bodies can develop rings. Now, thanks to the incredible sensitivity of the JWST, scientists know that the rings of Chariklo are even stranger than their initial discovery in 2013 suggested.
The team, led by researchers from the Institute of Astrophysics of Andalusia (IAA-CSIC), began observing Chariklo with the JWST in Oct. 2022. They used a technique called stellar occultation, which measures the decrease in light from a star when an object passes in front of it.
"By comparing JWST observations with those obtained during other stellar occultations over the last decade, we discovered opposite changes in the two rings: while the inner ring shows significantly higher opacity, the outer ring shows lower opacity," team leader Pablo Santos-Sanz of the IAA-CSIC said in a statement.
The changing rings of the asteroid suggest that it experiences more complex physics than previously thought. This is important because scientists had previously believed that small bodies had relatively stable rings.
"Our results force us to rethink how they form, how they evolve, and what mechanisms maintain their stability," Santos-Sanz said. "The ability to detect these changes opens a new window for understanding the evolution of these systems and, possibly, that of other ring systems in the solar system."
The cause of these changes remains a mystery.
Another milestone for the JWST and Gaia
The research doesn't just represent an important step in our understanding of asteroids and solar system rings, but it is also an important milestone for the JWST.
"Achieving this required knowing with extraordinary precision the orbit of Chariklo, the position of the star, thanks to the European Space Agency’s Gaia mission, and the trajectory of JWST itself around the L2 Lagrange point, a region of space located about 1 million miles (1.5 million kilometers) beyond Earth, away from the sun," team member Yücel Kilic of the IAA-CSIC said. "The JWST follows an orbit around this region that requires periodic corrections through station-keeping maneuvers."
 ![A black square with a lighter grey square inside it with a jagged orange line running across its base](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/2Cq96uXCEZz9Fv4uGFcvye.jpg) 
During the occultation the team used in their research, Chariklo was traveling at around 5,600 miles per hour (2.5 kilometers per second) relative to the JWST.
This is incredibly fast by Earth standards, but relatively slow for objects racing through the solar system. This low speed allowed the rings of Chariklo to be resolved in unprecedented detail. Astronomers currently rely on occultation to study Chariklo and its rings, as even the JWST isn't powerful enough to directly image this small and distant asteroid.
The team's research was published on Tuesday (Sept. 9) in the journal Science Advances.

He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. summary: Using the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers have discovered that the ring system surrounding the tiny solar system body Chariklo is changing over time. Observations revealed that Chariklo's inner ring has increased in opacity while its outer ring has decreased, challenging previous assumptions that small-body rings are stable. The exact cause of these changes remains a mystery, prompting scientists to rethink the formation and evolution of ring systems.
key_points: Chariklo is a small Centaur asteroid measuring about 155 miles wide and orbiting between Saturn and Uranus.
Researchers used the JWST and a technique called stellar occultation to observe changes in Chariklo's two thick rings.
Over a decade of observations showed opposite changes, with the inner ring showing higher opacity and the outer ring showing lower opacity.
The findings force scientists to rethink the physics, formation, and stability mechanisms of small solar system body rings.
Precise orbital data from the European Space Agency's Gaia mission and the JWST were critical to achieving these detailed observations.

title: Meteor shower season has begun – here’s how to watch in the UK
author: Rebecca Whittaker
content:
Meteor shower season is upon us, with longer, darker nights offering more opportunities to catch a glimpse of the wonders of the night sky.
In the coming months stargazers are set to be treated to an array of dazzling displays, including the Pleiades star cluster, Orionid meteor shower, a planetary parade and a supermoon this autumn.
Here, the Independent breaks down how to see these astral events and what to look out for.
![From early October to November the Orionid meteor shower is active](https://static.independent.co.uk/2025/10/20/17/06/iStock-1364432100.jpeg)
The Pleiades
A cluster of young stars called the Pleiades or the Seven Sisters will start to become prominent throughout autumn.
The stars which are around 440 light years away from Earth can be found by looking east. The Pleiades can be found in the constellation Taurus.
While you may assume there are only seven stars in the cluster, there are actually over 1,000, but only six are usually visible with the naked eye. But more can be seen when using a telescope.
Orionid meteor shower
From early October to November the Orionid meteor shower is already active.
The meteor shower, which can only be seen twice a year, reaches its peak around October 21.
It can be seen when Earth passes through debris left behind by Halley’s comet, which appears about every 75 years.
When these bits of debris enter Earth’s atmosphere they heat up and produce streaks of light.
November planetary parade
Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will all be aligned in the early morning sky on 14 November.
The four planets will be visible above the horizon before sunrise, but some will be easier to spot than others.
Venus and Jupiter are some of the brightest in the night’s sky and will be easier to see than Mercury which will stay low in the sky.
![The annual Leonid meteor shower and November supermoon](https://static.independent.co.uk/2024/11/15/12/meteor-shower-supermoon-date-november.jpg)
Leonid meteor shower
The Leonid meteor shower, which is one of the fastest meteors visible from Earth, is expected to peak by 17 November.
At the showers peak around 10 to 15 Leonids an hour can be visible, depending on weather, light pollution and the brightness of the Moon.
It’s named after the constellation Leo, where the meteors appear to radiate.
The Beaver supermoon
Another celestial treat will grace the skies in November with a supermoon.
November’s full moon is known as the Beaver Moon, which will be at its full phase on 24 November.
A supermoon occurs when the Moon is closer to Earth, making it look brighter and bigger.
summary: Meteor shower season has begun in the UK, offering stargazers longer and darker nights to view various celestial events. Upcoming autumn and winter highlights include the Pleiades star cluster, the Orionid and Leonid meteor showers, a planetary parade, and a November supermoon. These astral displays can be observed by looking toward specific constellations and regions of the night sky.
key_points: The Pleiades star cluster becomes prominent in autumn and can be found in the constellation Taurus.
The Orionid meteor shower is active from early October to November, peaking around October 21 due to debris from Halley's comet.
Mercury, Venus, Mars, and Jupiter will align in the early morning sky on 14 November.
The Leonid meteor shower peaks around November 17, offering 10 to 15 visible meteors per hour under good conditions.
The Beaver supermoon will reach its full phase on November 24, appearing bigger and brighter because the Moon is closer to Earth.

title: Europe will go it alone on Venus mission after NASA yanks radar instrument
author: Stephen Clark
content:
The European Space Agency is moving “full steam ahead” with development of a robotic mission to Venus after NASA officials determined they were unlikely to fulfill a commitment to provide a US-built radar instrument for the spacecraft, the mission’s project scientist said.
The European orbiter, named Envision, will map the Venusian surface at 10 times higher resolution than the last radar mission sent to Venus by NASA in the 1990s. The planet is enshrouded in a blanket of thick clouds of sulfuric acid, rendering its mysterious surface unseen by optical cameras in orbit. Radar is the most effective way to penetrate the clouds of Venus to reveal the terrain below, and scientists will use Envision to look for signs of active volcanism.
NASA and ESA signed a memorandum of understanding in 2024 outlining their partnership on Envision. NASA agreed to supply a US-made synthetic aperture radar instrument, Envision’s primary means of mapping the surface of Venus, along with providing tracking and communications support through NASA’s Deep Space Network. In exchange, ESA would include US researchers on Envision’s science team. Europe would build the Envision spacecraft and the rest of its science instruments and provide the launch on an Ariane 6 rocket.
But NASA’s budget for science missions is under the gun from the Trump administration, which proposed slashing the agency’s science funding nearly in half in fiscal years 2026 and 2027. Congress rejected most of the cuts in 2026, when lawmakers passed a budget with $2.54 billion for NASA’s planetary science division, far above the White House’s request, but about $220 million shy of last year’s funding.
That saved several key science missions from the chopping block, including one of NASA’s own Venus missions, called DAVINCI, designed to send an entry probe into the planet’s crushing atmosphere. But the shortfall is forcing NASA managers to make tough decisions. The primary targets for cuts in science are NASA’s funding for operating missions, especially those well beyond their original design lives, and support for partnerships on international missions.
summary: The European Space Agency is proceeding with its Envision mission to Venus independently after NASA determined it likely cannot provide a promised radar instrument. The partnership was established in a 2024 memorandum, but NASA's budget constraints and funding shortfalls have forced the agency to cut support for international mission partnerships. Despite budget pressures, NASA's own DAVINCI Venus mission was saved from cancellation.
key_points: The European Space Agency is moving forward alone with the Envision Venus orbiter mission.
NASA can no longer fulfill its commitment to provide a US-built radar instrument for Envision.
Budget constraints and funding shortfalls have forced NASA to reduce support for international mission partnerships.
NASA's own DAVINCI mission to Venus was saved from cancellation despite the budget pressures.

title: Your 80-year-old self will thank you for doing these 5 simple midlife exercises | BikeRadar
author: Rob Kemp
content:
For decades, ageing and physical decline were seen as inseparable. You hit middle age, energy dipped, joints stiffened and strength slipped slowly away. The accepted wisdom was it’s just what happens as you get older.
But a remarkable long–term Swedish study has challenged that fatalism – and reframed what ‘getting older’ means for your body.
Researchers at the Karolinska Institutet tracked adults for 47 years as part of the Swedish Physical Activity and Fitness (SPAF) project.
Rather than comparing different age groups, they repeatedly tested the same individuals over decades, measuring fitness, strength and muscular endurance.
The headline finding was sobering: physical performance begins declining around age 35, regardless of how fit you were in youth. From there, the drop is gradual but accelerates with advancing age.
Yet the more important discovery was encouraging. Participants who started exercising later in adulthood still improved their physical capacity by 5–10 per cent. In other words, ageing is inevitable but deterioration isn’t fixed.
“It is never too late to start moving,” said lead researcher Maria Westerstahl. Exercise may not stop decline completely, but it slows it meaningfully and preserves function.
That idea – preserving function – is the key distinction after 50.
The midlife wake–up call
![](https://www.bikeradar.com/resources/content/32337f2f-7841-4ef6-a233-d1f001580530/eaa5cdf4-608d-47d2-9a14-45e97b6795fa/b896579a-47b6-4777-8f46-47cf8a71de2b/Function-2.jpeg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=5f685598-5f4c-4683-adb3-f725b5018a2f)
Jason Smith knows this firsthand. Like many men in his 40s, he became busy, stressed and gradually less active. Lower energy felt normal. Strength loss felt expected. Age felt like the explanation. Turning 50 forced a choice: accept decline or push back.
Smith chose structured training: strength work, cardiovascular conditioning and mobility, and within months felt stronger, lighter and more capable than he had in years.
Now, he’s preaching what he practised through his Fit in Midlife coaching, working with middle–aged adults globally on maintaining independence and physical competence.
His philosophy mirrors the Swedish research: you’re not trying to stop ageing, you’re trying to stay functional. Strip training back to the essentials, and he says everything revolves around five movement patterns.
“Squat, hinge, push, pull and carry,” explains Smith. “Train those consistently and you’re not just exercising – you’re future–proofing.”
Below are the 5 exercises Smith considers non–negotiable after 50. Here’s how to do them and why they matter.
Squats: the independence exercise
![](https://www.bikeradar.com/resources/content/32337f2f-7841-4ef6-a233-d1f001580530/eaa5cdf4-608d-47d2-9a14-45e97b6795fa/e3a496bc-e407-446c-be40-40299971898f/Function-3.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=5f685598-5f4c-4683-adb3-f725b5018a2f)
What it trains: hips, knees, ankles, bone density.
Why it matters: the ability to stand up and sit down predicts long–term independence.
“The squat is arguably the most important movement in ageing well. It directly translates to getting out of chairs, climbing stairs and preventing falls.”
Method: stand feet shoulder–width apart. Push hips back and lean forward slightly. Keep spine neutral. Descend as low as comfortable. Stand back up under control. Start with bodyweight for 10–15 reps, then gradually add load.
Benefit after 50: loss of leg strength is one of the strongest predictors of frailty. “Squats load the skeleton, stimulating bone density and combating sarcopenia, that’s age-related muscle loss,” says Smith. They also improve balance and joint resilience – key factors in fall prevention.
Hip hinge (deadlift): protecting the back
![](https://www.bikeradar.com/resources/content/32337f2f-7841-4ef6-a233-d1f001580530/eaa5cdf4-608d-47d2-9a14-45e97b6795fa/81452f11-6a97-44cd-b106-5cf43e9e23d8/Function-4.png?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=5f685598-5f4c-4683-adb3-f725b5018a2f)
What it trains: glutes, hamstrings, lower back.
Why it matters: reduces risk of back pain and lifting injuries.
“Many midlife back problems stem from forgetting how to bend properly,” says Smith. “People round their spine instead of hinging at the hips.”
Method: hold kettlebells or dumbbells. Push hips backward. Keep chest tall. Lower weight toward floor. Drive hips forward to stand.
Benefit after 50: this movement builds what Smith calls your spinal ‘armour’. Strong posterior chain muscles stabilise the spine and make every-day lifting safer, from shopping bags to grandchildren. “It’s one of the highest–return exercises for functional longevity,” he adds.
Push–ups or chest press: upper–body preservation
![](https://www.bikeradar.com/resources/content/32337f2f-7841-4ef6-a233-d1f001580530/eaa5cdf4-608d-47d2-9a14-45e97b6795fa/ec959a2d-3907-4601-b8d6-39dfc557d6fc/Function-5.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=5f685598-5f4c-4683-adb3-f725b5018a2f)
What it trains: chest, shoulders, triceps.
Why it matters: upper-body strength declines fastest with age.
“Start with incline push-ups (hands on bench or wall), then progress to floor push-ups or a bench press.”
Method: shoulders down. Elbows at 45°. Controlled lowering.
Benefit after 50: after midlife, people rapidly lose pushing strength, affecting everything from opening doors to preventing falls. “Pressing movements maintain muscle mass and shoulder stability, both crucial for independence and injury prevention,” says Smith.
Rows or pull-downs: posture repair
![](https://www.bikeradar.com/resources/content/32337f2f-7841-4ef6-a233-d1f001580530/eaa5cdf4-608d-47d2-9a14-45e97b6795fa/52a3f3ea-778e-4d03-9a4c-1c10483c0e21/Function-6.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=5f685598-5f4c-4683-adb3-f725b5018a2f)
What it trains: upper back, biceps.
Why it matters: reverses desk and cycling posture.
“Years of sitting – and for cyclists, long hours in a forward-flexed position – weakens the upper back,” explains Smith.
Method: grip a bar or weight. Pull elbows toward ribs. Squeeze shoulder blades together. Lower slowly.
Benefit after 50: “Pulling exercises restore posture, reduce neck pain and protect shoulders. They also counteract the rounded–shoulder position strongly linked with reduced breathing capacity and higher injury risk.”
Farmer’s carries: real–world strength
![](https://www.bikeradar.com/resources/content/32337f2f-7841-4ef6-a233-d1f001580530/eaa5cdf4-608d-47d2-9a14-45e97b6795fa/a14e42ad-948f-42e5-b94a-647a48fe23ca/Function-7.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=5f685598-5f4c-4683-adb3-f725b5018a2f)
What it trains: grip, core, hips, shoulders.
Why it matters: grip strength predicts longevity. Grip strength is strongly correlated with overall health and mortality risk, making this deceptively simple movement incredibly valuable.
Method: pick up heavy dumbbells or kettlebells. Walk 30-40 metres. Keep an upright posture.
Benefit after 50: “Carries integrate the entire body and are the closest thing to real-life strength training.”
Why these movements beat complicated workouts
All of these exercises share something important: they are compound movements. “They use multiple joints, recruit multiple muscle groups and closely mirror the way humans actually move in daily life,” explains Smith. That matters more with every decade.
As we age, the body stops responding well to fragmented, isolation-style training. “Machines that train a single muscle might make it burn, but they don’t necessarily teach the body to function.
"Real life never asks you to contract one muscle at a time – it asks you to stand up, lift, reach, twist and stabilise all at once.”
That’s exactly what these patterns train. They load the skeleton, which helps maintain bone density and becomes crucial when fracture risk rises sharply in later life.
“They also stimulate large areas of muscle mass, counteracting sarcopenia, the age–related muscle loss that quietly reduces strength and metabolic health," says Smith.
"They reinforce coordination between muscles and joints, lowering fall risk, and they build usable, functional strength that preserves independence.”
When to do them
![](https://www.bikeradar.com/resources/content/32337f2f-7841-4ef6-a233-d1f001580530/eaa5cdf4-608d-47d2-9a14-45e97b6795fa/e0e976ba-bcf3-4c49-9ec1-b15ddabd2213/Function-8.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=5f685598-5f4c-4683-adb3-f725b5018a2f)
Train these movements three times a week and you will address most of the major physical threats associated with ageing in a single, efficient programme.
There are no complicated split routines, no endless variety – just repetition of patterns the body recognises and keeps.
“But strength alone isn’t enough,” adds Smith. “Without mobility, strong muscles eventually pull against stiff joints, and that’s where pain begins.
"Rather than chasing extreme flexibility, the aim after 50 is simply to maintain usable range of motion. A few short daily drills are usually enough to keep joints healthy and movement comfortable.”
Forward folds help maintain hamstring length and reduce tension in the lower spine. “A hip flexor stretch counters hours of sitting and often relieves lower-back discomfort,” says Smith.
“Thoracic spine rotations restore movement to the upper back, improving posture and shoulder mechanics. Deep squat holds keep hips, knees and ankles moving freely, while resistance-band pull–aparts maintain shoulder stability.”
The goal isn’t to become supple for its own sake – it’s to remain a physically capable adult who can move without restriction.
Don’t ignore intensity
High-intensity training still works after 50, and it remains extremely valuable for heart health and metabolic function. What changes is the dosage.
“Many of us can no longer train hard every day and expect the body to absorb it. Recovery capacity declines faster than work capacity,” adds Smith. So intelligent spacing of exercise and recovery matters more than raw effort.
A good guideline is one to two demanding sessions per week, ideally using joint-friendly drills such as cycling, rowing or uphill walking.
Warm-ups become essential rather than optional, and recovery – sleep, rest days and easier sessions – becomes part of the training itself.
There are also clear warning signs when intensity exceeds what the body can recover from: disrupted sleep, lingering joint aches, a rising resting heart rate and a sudden loss of motivation.
“After 50, progress rarely comes from punishment. It comes from consistency,” says Smith.
The long-term research shows improvement remains possible well into later life. In practice, however, the biggest early transformation people notice isn’t weight loss or endurance – it’s strength.
“Adding weight to a squat, completing a first push-up or carrying something heavy comfortably changes perception quickly,” adds Smith. “Instead of feeling fragile, people feel reliable in their own bodies again.”
Within a few weeks, posture improves, everyday movements feel easier and energy levels rise. That creates momentum, and momentum builds motivation far more effectively than willpower alone.
summary: While physical performance typically begins to decline around age 35, long-term research demonstrates that starting exercise in adulthood can still improve physical capacity and preserve function. Coach Jason Smith emphasizes that maintaining independence after 50 relies on five essential compound movement patterns: squats, hip hinges, push-ups, rows, and farmer's carries. Combining these strength exercises three times a week with proper mobility work, intelligent recovery, and occasional high-intensity training helps older adults build functional strength and prevent deterioration.
key_points: A long-term study by the Karolinska Institutet revealed that while physical decline begins around age 35, adults who start exercising later in life can still improve their physical capacity by 5 to 10 per cent.
Jason Smith's fitness philosophy for those over 50 focuses on preserving bodily function and independence rather than trying to stop the aging process entirely.
The five non-negotiable movement patterns for future-proofing the body are squats, hip hinges, pushes, pulls, and carries.
Compound movements are prioritized over isolation machines because they recruit multiple joints and mimic real-life physical demands.
Proper recovery, warm-ups, and intelligent spacing of high-intensity training are crucial after age 50 since the body's recovery capacity declines faster than its work capacity.

title: NASA, IBM launch new AI model for studying the moon
author: Julian Dossett
content:
![a grey, crater-marked orb on a black background](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/87Rn3PeiFZcAVm73TeQ25n.jpg) 
We've been studying the moon for a long time. NASA has gathered mountains of data over decades of lunar missions and studies. The data collected by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) alone, for example, exceeds that of all NASA's other planetary missions combined.
Analyzing all this information takes lots of time and effort from researchers. So, NASA and IBM have developed an AI model to help sift through the moon data — an advance the agency announced on Thursday (Sept. 10). The open-source model, called the NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model, is currently available for free at Hugging Face.
"NASA has spent decades building an extraordinary scientific record of the moon, but collecting data is only part of the job," NASA's Kevin Murphy, chief science data officer and acting chief data and AI officer, said in the announcement.
The new AI model can help researchers with tasks like mapping craters, finding young volcanic features, and modeling possible locations of water ice near the lunar poles, according to NASA.
In the announcement, Murphy said that NASA needs to make scientific data easier to explore and use. To this end, NASA has been developing and releasing science-focused AI models with IBM. Previous models include one focused on Earth observation and another for heliophysics.
This is part of a larger trend of AI use in planetary science. Space agencies and private space companies around the world have been looking into how AI models can help with analysis to increase scientific productivity, reduce costs and streamline workflows.
"The NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model shows what's possible when we bring AI to NASA's petabytes of scientific data," Murphy said in the announcement. "That's a real opportunity we see with AI: turning large-scale data into new discoveries."
The AI model was mostly trained on data from the LRO mission. Over 17 years, NASA's lunar orbiter has compiled a nearly complete mosaic of images that detail the moon's surface in high definition.

The NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model assists with tasks such as mapping craters, identifying young volcanic features, and modeling water ice locations near the poles. Trained primarily on data from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, the tool aims to make large-scale space data easier to explore and use.
