The AI tool is available for free at Hugging Face and was mostly trained on data from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.
It helps researchers map craters, find young volcanic features, and model potential water ice locations near the lunar poles.
This release is part of a broader trend of utilizing AI in planetary science to increase productivity and reduce costs.

title: The torch of the Statue of Liberty has been closed to the public since 1916, when German saboteurs blew up a munitions depot nearby and shrapnel tore into the statue's arm — in the 110 years since, no visitor has been allowed back up the ladder
author: Space Daily; Brendan Brown
content:
Every year, millions of people visit the Statue of Liberty, and a lucky, pre-booked fraction climb the 162 steps into her crown. What nobody gets to do — what nobody has done as a member of the public for 110 years — is continue upward, through the raised right arm, up the narrow 40-foot ladder into the torch.
The torch balcony, the statue’s actual summit, has been closed since 1916. Not for safety inspections, not for renovation. It is closed because of an act of war on American soil — one that most Americans have never heard of, carried out more than a year before the United States entered the First World War.
Two a.m., July 30, 1916
The target was Black Tom, a mile-long promontory and rail terminal jutting into New York Harbor from Jersey City, directly behind the Statue of Liberty. In 1916, neutral America was selling munitions to Britain and France by the shipload, and Black Tom was the funnel: on the night in question, its warehouses, rail cars and barges held roughly two million pounds of ammunition and explosives, waiting for transit to the Allied lines.
Imperial Germany, unable to stop the trade diplomatically, had built a sabotage network inside the United States to burn it instead. Shortly after two in the morning on July 30, 1916, small fires appeared on the terminal — set, as decades of investigation would establish, by German agents — and at 2:08 the depot went up in one of the largest man-made explosions the world had yet seen.
The blast has been estimated at the equivalent of a magnitude-5-class earthquake. It was felt as far away as Philadelphia and Maryland. Thousands of windows shattered across lower Manhattan and Jersey City; shrapnel and debris rained across the harbor; immigrants detained on Ellis Island had to be evacuated as fragments struck the buildings. The clock on the Jersey Journal building stopped at 2:12, holding the time of the explosion for decades. Remarkably, the confirmed death toll was small — a handful of people, including a railroad guard and an infant blown from his crib — a mercy owed entirely to the hour.
The statue takes shrapnel
The Statue of Liberty stood barely half a mile from the blast, facing it. The explosion drove chunks of steel into the statue and its island, peppering the copper skin; the damage, concentrated in the raised torch arm, was assessed at around $100,000 — well over $2 million today.
The arm had always been the statue’s engineering soft spot; its internal structure had been assembled slightly out of alignment in 1886, and officials had long eyed the torch climb nervously. The shrapnel settled the question. The ladder to the torch was closed to the public that year, and the closure simply never ended — through the statue’s 1938 refurbishment, through the 1980s centennial restoration, through every reopening of the crown, including the years-long closures after 9/11 and during later renovations. The crown always came back. The torch never did.
There is a wrinkle even in what “the torch” now means. The battered original — its flame rebuilt with glass panes in a 1916 repair by Gutzon Borglum, the future Mount Rushmore sculptor, which mostly succeeded in letting rain in — was finally taken down during the 1984–86 restoration and replaced with a new copper flame gilded in gold leaf. The 1886 original sits at ground level in the Statue of Liberty Museum, where visitors can finally stand next to the balcony their great-great-grandparents could climb into. The only people who go up the new torch’s ladder are National Park Service staff, to service the floodlights; a webcam on the balcony shows everyone else the view.
Germany pays, eventually
The other long tail of Black Tom was legal. Proving state-directed sabotage took decades of investigation through the German-American Mixed Claims Commission, tangled in denials, forged evidence and the small complication of a second World War. Germany was formally found responsible in 1939; a settlement of $50 million was agreed in 1953, and the final installments weren’t paid until 1979 — sixty-three years after the fires were lit. Black Tom itself was absorbed into landfill and is now a corner of Liberty State Park, marked by a modest plaque and a circle of flags that most picnickers walk past.
Which leaves the statue herself as the event’s most visible monument. The Black Tom explosion is a genuine historical hinge — it pushed Congress toward espionage legislation and helped shape the American intelligence apparatus — but its plainest legacy is subtractive: a missing experience. The most famous statue on Earth has an observation deck that has now been closed for 110 years and counting, sealed by an attack that predates the country’s entry into the war it belonged to. Every photograph of Liberty holding her torch above the harbor includes, unlabeled, the war damage: not a mark on the copper, but the emptiness of the balcony — a room shut in 1916 by men working for the Kaiser, and never reopened.
summary: The torch of the Statue of Liberty has been closed to the public since 1916 following a massive explosion at the Black Tom munitions depot in Jersey City. Caused by German saboteurs, the blast hurled shrapnel into the statue and severely damaged its already structurally vulnerable right arm. While the crown has reopened through various restorations over the decades, the ladder to the torch remains permanently off-limits to visitors.
key_points: The Statue of Liberty's torch balcony has been closed to the public since July 30, 1916.
The closure resulted from shrapnel damage caused by the Black Tom explosion, a massive munitions depot blast orchestrated by German saboteurs.
The damage compounded existing structural issues in the statue's raised right arm, prompting officials to close the ladder access indefinitely.
Germany was eventually held responsible for the sabotage, with final reparations settled in 1979.
Only National Park Service staff currently access the modern torch to service floodlights, while the original battered torch is displayed in the Statue of Liberty Museum.

title: How to get better at running without running, according to a top coach
author: Harry Bullmore
content:
It’s a familiar story: you want to get better at running so you start hitting a couple of hell-for-leather 5ks each week. But a few months in, your body feels beaten up and the time you’re running starts to plateau.
The primary fix is introducing a varied training week containing different types of runs to develop specific speed-boosting traits. But there are also ways you can improve your running ability without adding any extra running into your week, according to top endurance coach and Adidas ambassador Chris Hinshaw.
He describes these techniques as “cheat codes” of sorts – ways to better understand your body, get more out of it and improve your running capacity without racking up mile after mile.
Here are the three ways guaranteed to skyrocket your aerobic fitness, running ability and performance.
Mix modalities to reduce stress on the body
“The first thing someone needs to do [to get better at running] is develop their capacity,” Hinshaw explains.
“The risk is, if someone jumps straight into running regularly having not spent that much time on their feet before, they’re going to get hurt. So we devise ways – cheat codes, essentially – to build capacity in other movements that mimic the movement of running.”
Using an exercise bike is his go-to example. While running puts a significant amount of load through your lower body bones and joints, cycling can have you breathing hard “without creating the same structural damage”. However, it is more nuanced than simply saddling up and starting to pedal.
“When you run, you’re probably taking somewhere around 170 steps per minute,” says Hinshaw. Most fitness trackers will provide this information. Alternatively, you can run at your steady pace for 20 seconds, count the steps you take, then multiply this by three to get a good ballpark figure.
“If I put you on a bike, and we want the cadence to be identical to your running, 170 steps per minute is the equivalent of 85 revolutions per minute,” he adds.
Hinshaw recommends following a 30-minute cycle at this cadence with a 15-minute run at a sustainable pace – one at which you could comfortably hold a conversation.
“Now you’ve had 45 minutes of time under tension, cardiorespiratory adaptation and muscular stamina development, all while saving the knees, hips and ankles from too much joint stress” says Hinshaw. You have also had the chance to practice the skill of running and acclimatise your body to this higher impact activity.
Read more: How to start strength training and see results at any age, according to a top muscle growth expert
![Walking with a weighted rucksack, or rucking, raises the heart rate more than a standard stroll, leading to greater fitness adaptations](https://static.independent.co.uk/2024/09/13/09/WhatsApp-Image-2024-09-13-at-09.03.26.jpg)
Keep on rucking
Another way you can achieve this is through rucking – walking while carrying a weighted backpack.
The more weight you are moving, the harder your heart and lungs work to transport the nutrients needed to fuel your efforts. This is why rucking raises your heart rate more than a standard walk.
“I want you to carry roughly 10 per cent of your body weight, then we’re going to manipulate your cadence to deliver fitness benefits,” says Hinshaw.
“When you’re walking briskly, with intention, a normal cadence is about 115 to 125 steps per minute. If you carry a load at this higher pace, it’s going to put your heart rate in zone two, creating all the same respiratory adaptations as running, but through walking.”
The “beautiful” bonus benefit of this is it also creates structural adaptations, strengthening your bones, ligaments and tendons, adds Hinshaw.
Once again, he says, an effective protocol for those looking to shave down their 5k time would be to ruck for 30 minutes then finish with a 15-minute run.
“Your brain and your body are going to feel like they’ve just been for a 45-minute run, when in actual fact it was only 15 minutes,” says Hinshaw. “You are building capacity through these cheat codes, without having to do hours of running each week.”
Read more: Rucking is the fitness trend that’s here to stay – here’s why you should try it
![Switching out running for a lower impact aerobic activity like using an exercise bike can be a way to improve your fitness without putting as much stress on the body as you would while running](https://static.independent.co.uk/2025/12/23/15/37/iStock-1332406337.jpeg)
Focus on your breath – it can tell you when you’re in trouble
People tend to rely heavily on fitness trackers to tell them about the intensity of their workouts – usually via heart rate. But there is a better way, according to Hinshaw, which doesn’t involve dropping hundreds of pounds on an expensive wearable.
“The breath is the best way to monitor your workout intensity because it’s measuring your demand for oxygen,” says Hinshaw. “What happens when you increase the intensity of your workout? Your demand for oxygen goes up, so your heart rate rises to feed oxygen-rich blood to the moving muscles. We react to intensity, and our respiration rate changes.”
A lot can be learned from paying attention to how you are breathing during a workout. Is your breath fast or slow? Is it ragged or regular?
“When running, the exhale always occurs on a foot strike,” Hinshaw explains. “The most extreme form of breathing when running is called a two-count.” Here, you breathe in on one step, out on the next, then repeat the cycle.
“When you are in that situation, you are in deep trouble,” he continues. “You are going way too fast for your body to sustain this pace; you are accumulating massive amounts of lactate and it’s only a matter of time before your muscles shut down. Soon your only options will be to stop or slow down.”
Instead, for hard but sustained efforts like a 5k, Hinshaw teaches people to settle into a four-count breathing rhythm. Here, you inhale for three strides and exhale on the fourth.
“If you are running a 5k or Hyrox and, 600m in, you’re taking just two steps per cycle of breath, it’s time to slow down,” says Hinshaw. “The breath is the tell. It’s a way to assess yourself and your fatigue at any time during a run. Elite athletes use the breath to monitor intensity and pace. That’s why they win – because they’re smart.”
It works when gauging how much other runners have left in the tank too – handy when you’re feeling competitive at your local ParkRun. If those around you are breathing in and out with each stride, their pace will soon plummet. But if you are struggling to keep step with someone whose breathing is slow and controlled, they are going to be hard to beat.
Read more: The enjoyable exercise better than walking for lifelong fitness
![Aerobic capacity coach Chris Hinshaw teaching athletes how to learn their zone two breathing rhythm at the Adidas Go Full Hybrid event](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/08/14/20/Aerobic-capacity-coach-Chris-Hinshaw-teaching-athletes-how-to-learn-their-zone-two-breathing-rhythm.jpeg)
A two-count cycle of breath is universal among those approaching their physical limits, and a four-count breath can be applied to anyone working at a hard but sustainable pace. However, people’s breathing rates vary when running at a comfortable pace, often referred to as zone two due to the heart rate zone it corresponds to.
Walking is the best tool for determining your zone two breathing rate, Hinshaw advises.
“To find what works for you, it pays to play around with how many steps you take when you inhale and how many steps you take when you exhale,” he says. “You might take four steps on the inhale and four steps on the exhale. Or you might take as many as eight on each.
“What you’re doing here is developing the awareness of how your breath dovetails with your step rate. That’s why the military, when they ruck, are aware of their breathing rate and cadence. We need to take that mainstream and teach people how to do this.
“You want to be able to slow your breathing down, calm yourself and fill your lungs completely. This is supposed to be a low-stress, easy pace you can maintain for a long time. It’s not one size fits all. Your task is to identify the unique breathing rhythm that allows you to do this.”
Read more: I walked for 15 minutes after every meal for a month – the effects were immediate
summary: Endurance coach Chris Hinshaw shares expert techniques to improve running capacity and aerobic fitness without increasing running mileage, thereby reducing joint stress. His methods include cross-training with an exercise bike and rucking to build capacity while mimicking running mechanics. Additionally, he emphasizes using breathing rhythms to monitor workout intensity and pace effectively.
key_points: Using an exercise bike at a cadence matching your running steps helps build cardiorespiratory fitness while avoiding joint damage.
Rucking, or walking with a backpack weighted to about 10 percent of your body weight, raises the heart rate and builds structural strength similar to running.
Monitoring your breathing rhythm is a reliable, cost-free way to assess workout intensity and prevent burnout or premature fatigue.
A sustainable pace for hard efforts like a 5k relies on a four-count breathing rhythm, whereas a two-count rhythm indicates an unsustainable, overly intense pace.

title: Denisovans from southwestern China and their subsistence strategies - Nature
author: Ruan; Qijun; Hao; Xing; Song; Zhao; Keliang; Liu; Jianhui; Zanolli; Clément; Doyon; Luc; Delpiano; Davide; Peresani; Marco; D’Errico; Francesco; Demeter; Fabrice; Hublin; Jean-Jacques; Xiao; Peiyuan; Wang; Yuqing; Zhenxiu; Yang; Qingjiang; Fu; Qiaomei; Qiyahui; Yuhao; Lin; Sungui; Fan; Anchuan; Youping; Shao; Qingfeng; Bo; Chen; Fahu
content:
Abstract
Growing fossil and genomic evidence has substantially advanced our understanding of Denisovans’ evolutionary history1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9, yet their technological behaviours and subsistence strategies remain poorly documented. Here we present a comprehensive analysis of hominin fossils and associated archaeological remains from Bianfu Cave, Yunnan Province, southwestern China. The hominin fossils are dated to about 167–134 thousand years ago (ka), whereas the cultural sequence spanned from about 190 ka to 70 ka, representing one of the longest cultural records most parsimoniously attributed to Denisovans—identified through enamel–dentine junction morphology and palaeoproteomic analyses10. The new fossils include four teeth that expand the known dental variation of this group, two cranial fragments and a radius. Faunal and pollen records indicate a conifer-dominated forest or forest-steppe environment across Marine Isotope Stages 6 to 4. The inhabitants of Bianfu Cave practised specialized hunting of medium- to large-bodied prey and used a technological strategy characterized by expedient core reduction and tool production, alongside pervasive use of unmodified bones. This pattern suggests an adaptive system prioritizing the exploitation of object affordance over intensive tool manufacture. Bianfu Cave provides unprecedented insights into Denisovan biology, behaviour and ecology in eastern Asia and points to a substantial genetic and cultural legacy in later populations in Southeast Asia and Oceania.

summary: Researchers analyzed hominin fossils and archaeological remains from Bianfu Cave in Yunnan Province, southwestern China, dating the fossils to about 167–134 thousand years ago and the cultural sequence from roughly 190 to 70 ka. Identified as Denisovans through enamel-dentine morphology and palaeoproteomics, the finds include four new teeth, two cranial fragments, and a radius that expand known dental variation. Environmental records indicate a conifer-dominated forest or forest-steppe setting, where these Denisovan inhabitants engaged in specialized hunting of medium- to large-bodied prey and utilized an expedient tool production strategy.
key_points: Fossils and archaeological remains from Bianfu Cave in southwestern China provide one of the longest cultural records attributed to Denisovans.
The newly recovered hominin fossils include four teeth, two cranial fragments, and a radius, dated to roughly 167–134 ka.
Faunal and pollen data show that the inhabitants lived in a conifer-dominated forest or forest-steppe environment across Marine Isotope Stages 6 to 4.
The inhabitants practiced specialized hunting of medium- to large-bodied prey alongside an adaptive tool strategy prioritizing expedient core reduction and the pervasive use of unmodified bones.

title: Eats, sits and sleeps: scientists find cats are lazier than we think
author: Victoria Allen
content:
Looking on as your pet cat wakes from yet another luxurious nap, it can be hard not to feel a little envious. Now research has shown just how idle pet cats really are, finding that they only bother to walk less than 5 per cent of the time.
Scientists discovered that cats actually spend about three-quarters of their lives either lying or sitting down. They spend around 5 per cent of their time grooming themselves, and another 5 per cent eating.
The findings came from movement trackers, which recorded the secret lives of cats 24 hours a day for seven days in the summer, and again in the winter. The collar-worn trackers were given to 18 cats with outdoor access, and 10 indoor cats, to see how they spent their time.
In the summer, the outdoor cats spent 35 per cent of the time lying around, and 38 per cent of it sitting. That increased to 39 per cent of their time lying down in the winter, and 31 per cent of the time sitting.
Indoor cats spent 37 per cent of their time lying down in the summer, and 41 per cent of it sitting, with similar figures, 35 per cent and 41 per cent, for sitting and lying down in the winter.
Dr Michelle Smit, who led the study at Massey University in New Zealand, said: “One of the things owners were most curious about was what their cats were doing when nobody was watching.
summary: Recent research using movement trackers has revealed that pet cats spend about three-quarters of their lives either sitting or lying down. The study monitored 28 cats with both indoor and outdoor access over seven-day periods in summer and winter. Findings show that cats walk less than 5 percent of the time, devoting equal portions of their remaining schedule to grooming and eating.
key_points: Cats spend approximately 75 percent of their lives lying or sitting down.
Cats only walk less than 5 percent of the time.
Roughly 5 percent of a cat's time is spent grooming and another 5 percent eating.
The study monitored 18 outdoor cats and 10 indoor cats using collar-worn movement trackers.

title: The Atlantic Ocean Has a Hidden 'Heat Valve' That Controls Earth's Temperature – And It Could Be Closing
author: Starre Vartan
content:
Our relatively stable global climate is governed by an incredibly complex set of factors, all interacting with each other in dynamic and changeable ways – but there are a couple of really big, key players in that system.
The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is one of them.
This system of ocean currents redistributes heat from tropical regions up to cooler places, and cools warmer waters down too (important for sensitive marine life like corals).
Nutrients that ocean species rely on also get pushed around on this giant, mostly invisible conveyor belt beneath the waves.
Right now, the AMOC is weakening due to human-caused climate change, which could have huge repercussions, changing temperature and rainfall patterns humans rely on to grow food.
So it makes sense that researchers want to understand when and how, as lead author Christo Buizert writes in a research briefing, "a critical threshold beyond which AMOC weakening becomes self-reinforcing and irreversible."
That was the focus of a truly international team's study for Nature Geoscience that included Buizert.
(A fun note: Buizert was encouraged to submit this work to the journal after a chat over cheese fondue at a meeting in Switzerland. Proving that once again that giving scientists delicious free food is always a wise investment.)
Looking to the past might hold some answers: During the Pleistocene ice ages, the AMOC repeatedly switched between strong and weak states.
These shifts corresponded with abrupt climate events known as Dansgaard–Oeschger, or D–O, events, recorded particularly clearly in Greenland ice cores.
The conventional explanation for these D–O events was what the researchers call a "thermal bipolar seesaw." This climate seesaw was a model that seemed to explain how the AMOC-driven heat transport caused warming at one pole and cooling at the other pole.
Taking a new perspective, the researchers came up with another explanation which included "synthesizing two decades of observational and theoretical advances in understanding the crucial parts played by ocean heat content (OHC), sea ice, and the planetary radiation balance (the difference between the incoming solar radiation and outgoing radiation emitted by the Earth)," according to Buizert's statement.
Instead of thinking of the AMOC primarily as a conveyor belt shuttling heat from one hemisphere to another, researchers propose thinking of it more like an "ocean heat valve".
The researchers ran three climate models capable of producing spontaneous, self-sustaining D–O-like climate oscillations under glacial conditions.
They found that when the AMOC was strong, vigorous deep convection in the North Atlantic allowed the ocean to lose large amounts of heat to the atmosphere. The planet also lost energy to space.
When the AMOC weakened, deep convection shut down. The North Atlantic lost less heat than the rest of the ocean was absorbing, so heat accumulated in the ocean interior. The planet as a whole gained energy.
![The Atlantic Ocean's 'Heat Valve' Controls Earth's Temperature. Climate Change Could Weaken It.](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-10-at-1.02.53-AM-1083x675.png)
A conceptual diagram of the DO–OHC cycle, showing how Greenland and Antarctic temperatures track global ocean heat content as the AMOC switches between strong and weak states. (Buizert, et al. Nature Geoscience, 2026.)
In other words, the AMOC was acting less like a simple heat conveyor that moved heat from one place to another, and more like a valve controlling whether heat was allowed to escape from the ocean.
When the valve was open, heat drained out. When it was closed, heat accumulated.
This heat-valve model also helps explain a long-standing puzzle in varying ice-core records, which showed rapid changes in Greenland and slower changes in the Antarctic over the same time periods.
This new heat-valve model shows that this is due to the rapid changes in North Atlantic heat loss and slower changes in the amount of heat stored throughout the ocean, as reflected by the Antarctic records.
Rather than the two poles simply playing opposite ends of a heat-transfer seesaw, the researchers argue, both were responding to different aspects of a globally connected ocean heat cycle.
"The AMOC acts as an ocean heat valve regulating planetary temperature through Earth's radiative balance," wrote David Bonan, a climate scientist at the University of Washington, who provided an expert assessment of the work.
So, what happens in this valve model when applied to today's warming world?
As human-caused climate change alters the ocean, a weaker circulation could reduce deep convection and increase the amount of heat stored in the ocean. The researchers therefore conclude that future AMOC weakening could actually amplify planetary warming by "throttling down" the ocean heat valve.
![Subscribe to ScienceAlert's free fact-checked newsletter](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/05/FOMO-1200x628-_Dont-miss-the-next-breakthrough_-cosmic-colourful-642x336.jpg)
The researchers point out that their model gets an important asterisk:
The ice-age climate system was very different from today's. The D–O cycles occurred under glacial conditions, when enormous amounts of sea ice helped create the feedbacks that allowed the AMOC to flip between states. In a warmer future, the North Atlantic may be largely or entirely ice-free, removing a mechanism that was central to those ancient oscillations.
So the past doesn't provide a crystal ball for the AMOC's future. But it does offer something perhaps nearly as useful: a natural experiment showing that changes in this circulation can affect not just where heat goes, but how much heat the planet as a whole retains.
Buizert is calling for significantly more research into this because, as he writes, "Resolving whether the future AMOC has more than one stable state is a crucial research objective, because it might be the difference between transient weakening and an irreversible collapse, with profound societal implications."
The research has been published in Nature Geoscience.
summary: Researchers analyzing Pleistocene ice-age data have proposed a new "ocean heat valve" model for the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). Instead of simply moving heat between poles, the AMOC acts as a valve controlling whether heat escapes from the ocean into the atmosphere and space. The study suggests that human-induced weakening of the AMOC could reduce deep convection and trap more heat in the ocean, potentially amplifying planetary warming.
key_points: The AMOC is weakening due to human-caused climate change, which threatens temperature and rainfall patterns.
A new study published in Nature Geoscience reinterprets the AMOC as an "ocean heat valve" rather than a simple heat conveyor belt.
During ice ages, a strong AMOC allowed the ocean to release heat, while a weak AMOC caused heat to accumulate in the ocean interior.
Future AMOC weakening could amplify global warming by throttling down this ocean heat valve, though ice-age conditions differ from today's ice-free North Atlantic projections.

title: Experts just found an enormous volcano lurking under England | BBC Science Focus Magazine
author: Steph Santos Paulo
content:
Buried deep in the east coast of England, scientists have discovered an enormous ancient volcano several times more powerful than Mount Etna (pictured above).
The volcano, which lies under the counties of Norfolk and Lincolnshire, erupted with the force of several thousand hydrogen bombs 454.4 million years ago, blowing ash all the way to Scandinavia.
Researchers believe it is responsible for forming the ‘Kinnekulle tephra’ – an enormous bed of volcanic ash still found today across Norway, Sweden, the Baltic region, Belarus and Poland.
This remarkable discovery is “reshaping our understanding of England’s deep geological past”, said Dr Tim Pharaoh, a geophysicist at the British Geological Survey and lead author of the study.
The clues that this previously hidden volcano existed lay in rock samples taken from two boreholes spaced 65km (40.4mi) apart in Norfolk and Lincolnshire.
But the ancient volcano may have spanned an area far bigger than 65km.
“This was probably not a simple, cone-shaped volcano,” said Dr Dan Condon, a research scientist at the British Geological Survey who co-authored the study.
He told BBC Science Focus that the evidence points to a large and complex volcanic system containing several cauldron-like hollows – known as ‘calderas’ – extending across tens of kilometres above an extensive body of magma.
The researchers analysed tiny particles embedded in the ancient volcanic rock – known as zircon crystals – which enabled them to calculate the volcano’s age “at the highest levels of precision currently achievable”.
“Zircon crystals act as tiny natural clocks,” explained Condon. When zircon crystallises from magma, it incorporates uranium into its structure, which over time changes into lead.
By measuring the rate of this change, Condon and his team discovered that the rock in the ancient English volcano and the Kinnekulle tephra in northern Europe formed at the same time.
As well as calculating their age, they analysed the composition of the rock samples and found that their ‘chemical fingerprints’ also matched.
“Trying to estimate the size of eruptions we have not witnessed is like trying to guess the picture on a jigsaw puzzle with only a few bits in place,” said Prof Jenni Barclay, a volcanologist at the University of Bristol who was not involved in the study.
This study finds striking similarities in the age and composition of rocks located hundreds of miles apart, making us, according to Barclay, “more certain these pieces are from the same eruption”.
Read more:
summary: Scientists have discovered a massive ancient volcano buried beneath the counties of Norfolk and Lincolnshire in England. Erupting 454.4 million years ago with immense force, the complex volcanic system is believed to have created the widespread 'Kinnekulle tephra' ash bed found across northern Europe. Researchers confirmed the connection by analyzing the precise age and chemical fingerprints of zircon crystals in rock samples from boreholes.
key_points: An enormous ancient volcano has been discovered buried under Norfolk and Lincolnshire in England.
The volcano erupted 454.4 million years ago with the force of several thousand hydrogen bombs.
Researchers linked the volcano to the 'Kinnekulle tephra' ash bed found across Scandinavia and the Baltic region.
The discovery was made by analyzing the age and chemical composition of zircon crystals from rock boreholes.

title: Osteoporosis affects millions: could modified cells rebuild their bones?
author: Dolgin; Elie
content:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
and JavaScript.
Osteoporosis causes thin, porous bones that are prone to fracture, but a promising cell therapy might offer a way to strengthen them.Credit: Dr Tony Brain/SPL
The ten older women had, between them, broken their bones dozens of times, often after little more than a stumble. But after receiving a single infusion of their own bone-marrow cells, treated in the laboratory to help the cells penetrate bone tissue, the women’s fractures all but stopped.
Before treatment, the women — the participants of small clinical trial reported1 today in Cell — experienced fractures in their spines, hips, arms and other bones every year or two, on average. After the trial, the women experienced bone breaks caused by low-impact trauma at a rate closer to once per decade.
The results raise the tantalizing possibility that a one-time cell therapy could rebuild brittle bones in people with osteoporosis, an ageing-related condition that affects around 200 million women worldwide, particularly after menopause.
“It’s quite remarkable,” says Ajit Varki, a physician-scientist at the University of California, San Diego who was not involved in the study. The trial “showed an almost 100% efficacy sustained for several years — and no side effects”.
Still, the findings come with hefty caveats. The study was small, had no control group and most of its participants were taking conventional osteoporosis drugs before and during the trial, making it difficult to tease out the effects of the cell therapy.
What’s more, the researchers did not directly track the therapeutic cells in the recipients’ bodies, leaving a crucial question unanswered: did enough of the cells reach the bones to make a difference?
Straight to the bone
Robert Sackstein, a regenerative-medicine specialist at the Miami Veterans Affairs Medical Center in Florida and a co-author on the study, is confident that they did. Sackstein has spent decades studying how various cells with regenerative potential — including bone-forming progenitor cells known as mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) — can be steered through the body for maximal therapeutic effect.
MSCs, when injected into the bloodstream, cannot usually reach bone tissue. But in 2008, Sackstein and his colleagues found that adding a sugar called fucose to these stem cell-like cells enabled them to seek out and enter bones, leading to skeletal tissue generation in mice2.
The added sugars usually disappear within about two days, and are thought to work by fostering interactions between the MSCs and blood-vessel walls. Those interactions slow the cells, allowing them to squeeze into the bone marrow.
After seeing the approach work in mice, Sackstein and his colleagues turned their attention to humans. According to the authors, few trials had tested MSCs for osteoporosis, and no trials in any disease had deliberately modified the cells to improve their trafficking ability. It took several years to fine-tune the manufacturing process3 and generate the required preclinical data before the trial could proceed.
But finally, in 2015, clinical collaborators in Spain led by bone-marrow transplant specialist José Moraleda at the University of Murcia, began the trial. They treated women aged 51 to 72, who had advanced osteoporosis and a history of fractures, with MSCs extracted from their own bone marrow and enhanced with fucose.

summary: A small clinical trial found that a single infusion of modified bone-marrow cells dramatically reduced bone fractures in ten older women with advanced osteoporosis. The therapy involves treating the patients' mesenchymal stromal cells with a sugar called fucose to help them penetrate bone tissue. While experts call the results remarkable, researchers note important caveats, including the study's small size, lack of a control group, and concurrent use of conventional drugs.
key_points: Ten older women with severe osteoporosis received a single infusion of their own bone-marrow cells treated with fucose.
The treatment reduced the rate of low-impact bone breaks from once every one to two years down to roughly once per decade.
Adding fucose to mesenchymal stromal cells helps them interact with blood-vessel walls and enter bone marrow.
The clinical trial was small and lacked a control group, leaving questions about the direct impact of the therapy.
Participants were also taking conventional osteoporosis drugs during the trial.

title: A star is exploding 45 million light-years away — here's how you can see it
author: Jamie Carter
content:
![graphic illustration of a large supernova explosion in space.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/wf94QDTXPRLRTH2YeoJZdE.jpg) 
An extraordinary exploding star has been spotted in a distant galaxy, and astrophotographers are racing to capture it before it fades from view.
The supernova, called SN 2026aaiv, was first seen by the ATLAS survey on Sept. 1 in NGC 7331 (also known as Caldwell 30), a spiral galaxy about 45 million light-years away in the constellation Pegasus, visible in the Northern Hemisphere and at mid-latitudes in the Southern Hemisphere.
That makes this supernova a prime target for amateur astrophotographers and astronomers worldwide to capture an image of this rare event.
Hundreds of astrophotographers have already captured it, including Andrew McCarthy, who posted his image on Instagram on Sept. 7 with the message, "As luck would have it, I happened to be in the middle of a massive project with this galaxy, and caught the supernova." He shot four hours of data, two before and two after the supernova, as part of a 100-hour project. "The final image will be EPIC!" he said.
Tom Masterson, Mountain Operations Manager at the Mount Wilson Observatory, also captured it on Sept. 10 using a 60-inch telescope.
What you'll need to find SN 2026aaiv
At magnitude 15.7 on Sept. 11, 2026, SN 2026aaiv is relatively dim, but still brightening. Many of the images posted online were captured with large professional telescopes or remote telescopes in dark regions. However, you can find and photograph SN 2026aaiv with relatively modest equipment. You'll need a telescope or large binoculars to see NGC 7331 (at magnitude 10) at all, but the supernova is dramatically more challenging visually. To have a chance of seeing SN 2026aaiv, a large telescope is recommended (observers have confirmed seeing it using a 14-inch Schmidt-Cassegrain telescope). Use the averted vision technique: look slightly to the side of the galaxy's core so the eye's more light-sensitive rod cells can reveal faint detail.
The easiest way is to use a smart telescope, which can quickly find and image the host galaxy NGC 7331. According to Seestar (Official ZWO Group) on Facebook, users of the Seestar S50 have managed to image the SN 2026aaiv with about two hours of 10-second exposures (the default mode).
How to find SN 2026aaiv
 ![night sky graphic map showing the great square of pegasus](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/FEpkw2ipDqombN6ih8oJk.jpg) 
SN 2026aaiv has the coordinates RA 22h 37m 05.618s, Dec +34° 24′ 35.37″. From the Northern Hemisphere, turn toward the east after dark, and you'll see four large, bright stars rising in a vast diamond shape. This is the Great Square of Pegasus, part of the constellation Pegasus. At the northwestern corner of the Great Square is Scheat. Just above it, outside the square, is a dimmer star called Matar. NGC 7331 is close by. In light-polluted skies, only the central core of the galaxy is visible, according to NASA. The galaxy, which we see partially edge-on, has spectacular spiral arms that swirl around a bright central region.
What we know about SN 2026aaiv
SN 2026aaiv is a Type Ia supernova, a catastrophic explosion that occurs when a white dwarf in a binary star system gains enough material from its companion to trigger a runaway thermonuclear reaction, destroying the white dwarf. Remarkably, another Type Ia supernova, SN 2025rbs, was found in the same galaxy on July 14, 2025.
NGC 7331, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope in 2018, was first found in 1784 by British astronomer William Herschel, who cataloged over 2,500 deep-sky objects and discovered Uranus and its two largest moons. NGC 7331 is similar in size, shape and mass to the Milky Way.

![Jamie Carter](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/MffDhM2CVPnTub5sutYwga.jpg) 
Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.
summary: A rare supernova named SN 2026aaiv has been spotted in the spiral galaxy NGC 7331, located approximately 45 million light-years away in the constellation Pegasus. First detected on September 1 by the ATLAS survey, the Type Ia supernova is currently brightening and has become a popular target for astrophotographers worldwide. Observers can locate the galaxy near the constellation Pegasus using telescopes, smart telescopes, or large binoculars.
key_points: The supernova SN 2026aaiv is located in the NGC 7331 galaxy, about 45 million light-years away.
It is a Type Ia supernova caused by a runaway thermonuclear reaction on a white dwarf.
Observers can find the host galaxy near the Great Square of Pegasus in the Northern Hemisphere.
While dim at magnitude 15.7, it has been successfully captured by both professional astrophotographers and smart telescopes.

title: AI researchers reckon with the $1.5 million ‘academia tax’
author: Deighton; Ben
content:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
and JavaScript.
AI researchers reckon with the $1.5 million ‘academia tax’
Academics explain that their research freedom beats the increased salary they would get in the corporate sector, but emerging hybrid models might allow them to get the best of both worlds.
Artificial-intelligence researchers say that the idea of leaving academia is tempting, but some nevertheless resist the move.Credit: Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty
If you’re looking to make money with your skills in artificial intelligence, academia isn’t the most lucrative destination. The National Bureau of Economic Research in Cambridge, Massachusetts, conducted an analysis1 of AI researchers and identified those with similar specialisms across academia and the private sector. They found that the top 1% of industry authors earn US$1.5 million more per person every year than do their academic counterparts.
Nature spoke to academics, mostly in the United States and Europe, and many mentioned students who have gone to work for firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI, both in San Francisco, California, and earn millions of dollars a year. Despite that, those who remain in academia say that the freedom to choose their research and the joy of training the next generation trumps the increased salaries of industry, though many still gripe about the issues they face in finding stable funding streams.
Source: United States’ National Bureau of Economic Research
Increasingly, however, researchers are adopting hybrid roles in which they split their time between technology companies and university research, getting the benefits of both.
Here, 14 university academics who specialize in AI and computational science share their reasons for staying in academia and the factors that might push them into industry.
The freedom to choose
“I’m not yet convinced that the extra money is worth the loss of the ability to do research in the areas you find interesting in the long term. It’s a thing that you possibly don’t get in industry — in academia, you could have projects going for a decade.” — Stewart Clark, computational physicist at Durham University, UK
“As scientists and educators, academia gives us an unusual amount of freedom to decide what questions we want to work on and what we think matters. I think that’s tremendously powerful.” —Jian Ma, computational biologist at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania
“If I decide tomorrow to completely shift the area of research I’m working on, no one can stop me doing that. If you are in a company, it’s a completely different game. When you are leading an academic research laboratory, you are completely at the steering wheel and the freedom that you get there is very special.” — Dima Damen, computer scientist at the University of Bristol, UK, and at Google DeepMind.
Working and publishing openly
“A lot of people have bought into the idea that if you want to be on the cutting edge, you have to be at one of the big companies. But for me, I think it’s important that someone has the role of doing the work out in the open, reporting on experiments, reporting what works, what doesn’t and sharing artefacts that can be used by anyone to do scientific study or adaptation.” — Noah Smith, AI researcher at the University of Washington in Seattle
Mentoring the next generation
“The impact you can have from teaching is amazing. I still get e-mails from students from my early years of teaching. You get that more personal view of your impact on society.” — Ivor Simpson, informatics researcher at the University of Sussex in Brighton, UK
“Three of my former PhD students are now faculty members. And I think that’s my greatest achievement, much more than research, because the research you do is going to be state-of-the-art today, but it’s not a legacy.” — Damen
“Seeing doctoral students progress is the key thing for me. When you’re holding meetings with them, they’re the experts and they know more than anybody else about the subject of their dissertation. And they go out into the world and make an impact. It’s a real pleasure to see that academics contribute to the world in this way.” — Gaurav Sukhatme, computer scientist at the University of Southern California, Los Angeles
It’s not just about money
“When I first moved back to academia, a lot of my friends from my PhD and from wider life were asking me why I was doing this. They said, ‘Are you mad? You’re losing a huge amount of salary.’ And this is something that obviously hasn’t recovered, because you don’t get paid very well as an academic. A lot of my undergraduates will go off and get paid more than I do, which is disappointing. However, I wanted my research to have impact beyond the generation of revenue. I think that that’s the main thing, as well as having a little bit more control over what it could be applied to.” — Simpson
“There are some roles in industry, such as managerial research and development, that are quite interesting. But I would say that I’ll think very carefully before trading the freedom I have to collaborate for a managerial role. Then you have to abandon science and I am enjoying it too much so far.” — Paola Carbone, computational chemist at the University of Manchester, UK
“The amount of money that these guys are making at Anthropic and OpenAI is just mind‑boggling — from being my student two years ago to making US$2 million a year. Then again, they basically say, ‘If I have my job for five years, I’m going to be lucky’, because they see that they’re literally training the large language models that are going to replace them. So, they can see the end of the road.” — Peter Nugent, physicist at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, California
“It’s definitely not all about the money. In my case, I think I can offer a unique perspective: I had the money. When I was working in investment banking, it was crazy; the hours are crazy. We have deadlines, and academics still have to work really hard, but the hours in banking were a different level.” — Vandana Dwarka, mathematician at Delft University of Technology, the Netherlands

summary: An analysis by the National Bureau of Economic Research reveals that the top 1% of private-sector artificial-intelligence authors earn $1.5 million more annually than their academic counterparts. Despite these significantly higher industry salaries, many academic researchers choose to remain in universities for the freedom to choose their research topics, the ability to work and publish openly, and the joy of mentoring students. To capture the best of both worlds, an increasing number of researchers are adopting hybrid roles that split time between tech companies and universities.
key_points: The top 1% of AI industry authors earn $1.5 million more per person each year than academics in the same specialisms.
Many academic researchers value the freedom to choose their own long-term research topics over higher corporate salaries.
Academics highlight the importance of working in the open and mentoring the next generation of students.
Some researchers are adopting hybrid roles that allow them to split their time between technology companies and universities.

title: Astronomers used 69 fast radio bursts as cosmic backlights to complete the clearest census yet of the universe’s missing ordinary matter, finding that roughly 76% resides as extremely diffuse ionized gas in the vast spaces between galaxies — while only 9% remains inside galaxies as stars and gas.
author: Space Daily; Deep Field
content:
The universe’s “missing matter” was never thought to have vanished. Cosmologists could infer how much ordinary, atom-building matter should exist, but direct inventories of stars, cold gas and the hot gas in galaxy clusters did not recover all of it in the nearby universe. The discrepancy pointed instead to matter that is real, widespread and exceptionally difficult to see.
A census built from 69 precisely located fast radio bursts now places most of that elusive material in the thinnest part of the cosmic web. In a study published on 16 June 2025 in Nature Astronomy, Liam Connor and colleagues estimate that 76 per cent of ordinary matter lies in the intergalactic medium, with an uncertainty of plus 10 and minus 11 percentage points. About 15 per cent lies in extended galactic halos, while 9 per cent is in stars and cold galactic gas.
This is one study, not settled consensus. Its fractions are a statistical inference from a modest sample, foreground estimates and a model of where electrons reside. They are not a direct count of individual particles. Even so, the work makes a more discriminating partition of the late-universe baryon budget than earlier fast-burst measurements could provide.
The missing matter was ordinary
In cosmology, baryons are the family of ordinary particles that includes protons and neutrons, the ingredients of atomic nuclei. Measurements of the early universe, including the Planck cosmic microwave background analysis, tightly constrain how many baryons the cosmos contains. Big Bang nucleosynthesis reaches a compatible answer through the primordial abundances of light elements.
Yet stars are bright rather than abundant. Add stellar mass, cold galactic gas, hot cluster gas and other detectable reservoirs, and the local tally historically came up short of that early-universe prediction. The leading expectation was that much of the difference occupied the warm-hot intergalactic medium, spread through filaments so thinly that its emission and absorption signatures were hard to assemble into a complete census. Individual detections existed, but extrapolating them across an inhomogeneous cosmic web left substantial room between locating some of the reservoir and measuring its global share.
The 76/15/9 division is therefore not a breakdown of everything in the universe. It partitions ordinary matter alone. Dark matter is a separate, non-baryonic component, and dark energy belongs to the wider mass-energy budget. Ordinary matter makes up only about one-sixth of all matter, so 76 per cent of baryons is not 76 per cent of all cosmic matter.
How a millisecond burst weighs invisible gas
A fast radio burst, or FRB, is a brief flash of radio energy from a distant galaxy. Its physical source may differ from event to event, but that uncertainty does not prevent an FRB from working as a probe. What matters for the census is the signal’s journey through intervening plasma.
Ionized gas contains free electrons. When a burst passes through it, lower radio frequencies arrive slightly later than higher ones. The size of this frequency-dependent delay yields the dispersion measure, which is proportional to the column of free electrons integrated along the full sightline. Gas that is far too faint to photograph can still leave a measurable timing signature.
Distance turns that electron column into a cosmological tool. Once astronomers identify a burst’s host galaxy and measure its redshift, they can compare how far the signal travelled with how much plasma it encountered. They must also estimate the contributions from the Milky Way, the host galaxy and intervening galactic halos before attributing the balance to intergalactic space.
Why localization mattered
A burst without a securely identified host is much less useful because its distance remains uncertain. Thirty-nine of the 69 events in the study came from the Deep Synoptic Array-110 at California’s Owens Valley Radio Observatory. The array was designed not merely to detect FRBs, but to pinpoint them accurately enough for follow-up observations of their host galaxies.
The other 30 bursts came from telescopes around the world, primarily the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder. Optical observations from facilities including the Keck and Palomar observatories helped establish host redshifts. That combination, a radio dispersion measure tied to a known cosmic distance, is the essential unit in the analysis.
According to Caltech’s account of the project, the 69 localized bursts ranged from about 11.74 million to 9.1 billion light-years away. The most distant was FRB 20230521B. The long baseline supplied both nearby and remote probes of the accumulated electrons between galaxies rather than relying on a narrow slice of cosmic history.
The 76 per cent is an inference with error bars
The team’s intergalactic category means gas outside virialized galaxy halos, combining filaments and voids. The published estimate assigns 76 per cent of baryons to this reservoir, with a plus 10 and minus 11 percentage-point uncertainty. The central value is memorable, but the interval is part of the result and should travel with it.
The same analysis describes this gas as highly ionized and extremely diffuse. Its density is below roughly 0.001 particles per cubic centimetre, and its neutral fraction is below one part in 10,000. Those limits explain the observational problem: the gas can dominate the ordinary-matter inventory while producing little light of its own.
The remaining shares are about 15 per cent in the extended halos around galaxies and 9 per cent in stars and cold galactic gas. These are fitted population fractions, not three piles weighed independently. The open preprint record describes how simulations help calibrate the statistical fingerprints of the different components, including the uneven contributions from intervening halos.
What changed after the first FRB census
The crucial groundwork was the 2020 Macquart relation, named for the late astronomer J. Xavier Prochaska Macquart. Using a smaller set of localized bursts, that study showed that dispersion increases with redshift in a way consistent with the expected cosmic density of baryons. FRBs could recover the missing total.
Recovering the total was not the same as assigning matter to environments. The average dispersion-redshift trend mainly constrains how many baryons exist along the line of sight. Separating smooth intergalactic gas from the clumpier material around galaxies requires information in the distribution and scatter of individual measurements, plus knowledge of which foreground halos a sightline crosses.
The 69-burst analysis combines those clues. Diffuse gas produces a relatively smooth accumulation with distance, while halos add irregular contributions on selected sightlines. A previous SpaceDaily report on a record-distance localized FRB explains why reaching farther into the universe extends the lever arm for this kind of measurement.
A clue about galaxy feedback
If roughly three-quarters of baryons are outside halos, galaxies have not retained all the gas that gravity drew toward them. Supernovae, stellar winds and accreting supermassive black holes can heat gas and drive it outward. In simulations, the strength of that feedback determines how much material remains near galaxies and how much is expelled into the broader web.
The study argues that relatively efficient feedback is needed to reproduce the inferred split. That gives galaxy-formation models a new observational constraint: matching the number and appearance of galaxies is not sufficient if a simulation stores too much ordinary matter inside their halos. The baryon census tests the otherwise faint aftermath of billions of years of outflows.
Redistributed gas also changes how matter clusters on intermediate scales. The authors note that stronger baryonic feedback could reduce part of the S8 tension, a mismatch between some early- and late-universe estimates of clustering amplitude. That is a possible implication rather than a demonstrated resolution, and it depends on whether the inferred gas distribution survives larger and more varied FRB samples.
A census, not a map of every particle
The method is powerful precisely because electrons that are almost invisible in emission still delay radio waves. Its limitations follow the same line of reasoning. Each burst mixes contributions from the Milky Way, intergalactic space, foreground halos and its host. Errors in any of those components can shift the inferred partition even if the measured dispersion itself is precise.
Selection also matters. Only localized bursts with usable host information enter this kind of census, and that subset may not perfectly represent the full FRB population. The conversion from observed scatter to environmental fractions depends on halo prescriptions and on simulations such as IllustrisTNG. The quoted uncertainties reflect the statistical model, but no error bar can guarantee that every modelling assumption is complete.
Sixty-nine events are enough to sharpen the fractions, not enough to erase every degeneracy. Future arrays should supply thousands of localized sightlines, allowing the budget to be tested across redshift, galaxy type and foreground environment. The clearest conclusion for now is deliberately bounded: most ordinary matter long missing from visible inventories is consistent with very diffuse, ionized gas between galaxies.
summary: Using 69 precisely located fast radio bursts as cosmic backlights, astronomers have completed a clear census of the universe's ordinary matter, or baryons. The study estimates that roughly 76% of this matter resides as extremely diffuse ionized gas in the intergalactic medium, while 15% is in extended galactic halos and 9% is inside galaxies as stars and cold gas. This statistical inference provides a more detailed partition of the late-universe baryon budget than previous measurements, though it relies on modeling and statistical scatter rather than direct particle counts.
key_points: Roughly 76% of ordinary matter is located in the intergalactic medium as diffuse, highly ionized gas.
About 15% of baryons reside in extended galactic halos, and 9% remain inside galaxies as stars and cold gas.
The census relies on measuring the frequency-dependent timing delays, or dispersion measures, of 69 localized fast radio bursts traveling from distant host galaxies.
The 76% intergalactic share is a statistical inference with an uncertainty of plus 10 and minus 11 percentage points.
The findings suggest that galaxy feedback mechanisms, such as supernovae and black holes, have efficiently expelled gas outward from galaxies into the wider cosmic web.

title: "The more aroused the fly is the harder it tries to shoot" - Google's fully mapped fly brain is now playing Doom, Beat Saber, and more
author: Robert Purchese
content:
It's science-fiction Friday as Google's fully mapped fly brain, which was revealed last week, has been engineered to play Doom and rhythm-action game Beat Saber.
Google's brain-mapping is a historic first and the model of the fly brain - which took years of work and AI-help to compile - was released by the company's research team and made available for download. A few days later, as reported by PC Gamer, this resulted in the brain being trained to play Doom.
"I'm training a fly brain to play Doom using the full MaleCNS v1.0 fruit fly connectome," announced Coinbase engineer Alex Wormuth, who also published a live video feed of the simulated fly's progress. Apparently it played thousands of times and is still not doing very well.
Not long after, another enterprising engineer, domi on Bluesky, got the fly brain playing lightsaber-based rhythm-action game Beat Saber. A video shows a little fly model waving the lightsabers around and slicing through advancing tiles, probably better than I would.
The same modder got the fly brain playing shooters, using the fly's brain to work out when to turn, apparently, and its "courtship song" for when to shoot. "The more aroused the fly is the harder it tries to shoot," domi noted, alarmingly.
Google had already successfully mapped the brain of a female adult fruit fly, but this time it's a male fruit fly's brain that's been mapped - and as Google pointed out, there's a notable difference. "It's a big step in advancing neuroscience experiments", Google said, perhaps envisioning it running on Doom, "and promises to be a foundational resource for neuroscience for years to come".
summary: Following Google's release of a fully mapped male fruit fly brain connectome, engineers have successfully trained the simulated brain to play video games like Doom and Beat Saber. Coinbase engineer Alex Wormuth used the MaleCNS v1.0 connectome to train the fly brain to play Doom, while another engineer got it playing Beat Saber and shooters. Google views this historic brain-mapping achievement as a foundational resource that will advance future neuroscience experiments.
key_points: Google and its research team released a fully mapped model of a male fruit fly brain for public download.
Engineer Alex Wormuth trained the simulated fly brain to play Doom using the MaleCNS v1.0 connectome.
Modder domi successfully programmed the fly brain to play Beat Saber and other shooter games.
Google considers the detailed brain mapping a historic milestone and a foundational resource for advancing neuroscience.

title: One giant step: first known adult T rex footprints found in North Dakota
author: Oliver Milman
content:
The first known series of footprints from an adult Tyrannosaurus rex has been found in North Dakota by a team of scientists.
The 23ft-long trackway – consisting of four three-toed footprints, two left and two right – was first identified in the south-west of the state, in the dinosaur fossil area known as Hell Creek Formation, last year by researchers from the Denver Museum of Nature and Science in Colorado and Liverpool John Moores University in the UK.
The findings, which have now been published in a scientific journal, date from 66.5m years ago and are the first of their kind to be found and identified. While isolated footprints and juvenile, or related species, tracks have been found before, this is the first known series of footprints left by a wandering T rex.
“Bones tell us an enormous amount about these animals, but footprints capture a moment of behavior,” said Tyler Lyson, senior curator of vertebrate paleontology at the Denver museum.
“With a trackway, we can actually follow an animal as it moved across the landscape. That is incredibly rare for T rex.”
Each of the footprints is about 3ft (0.91m) long, with a stride of about 13ft (3.96m). The research team used high-resolution 3D surface scanning to document each footprint and create physical 3D reproductions. From this work, researchers were able to make a rough estimate that the animal was walking about 3.5-4.5mph – about the same as a brisk human walking pace.
The T rex, the most famous of all dinosaurs, lived about 66-68m years ago during the Cretaceous period, according to the known fossil record. The creatures, which stood 12-13ft tall, were among the last non-avian dinosaurs to walk the Earth before a mass extinction event wiped them out.
Three of the discovered footprints are set to be recovered by helicopter later this year and transported to the museum in Denver. The findings are a particular joy for the Colorado schoolteacher who stumbled upon the site.
“As a teacher, I’m always telling my students that science starts with curiosity, passion and careful observation,” said Kent Hups, who is a longtime museum volunteer and also co-authored the paper. “I never imagined that could lead me to a discovery like this.”
summary: Scientists in North Dakota have discovered the first known series of adult Tyrannosaurus rex footprints in the Hell Creek Formation. The 23-foot-long trackway, dating back 66.5 million years, consists of four three-toed prints that allow researchers to study the dinosaur's movement and behavior. Using 3D scanning, researchers estimated the T. rex was walking at a brisk human pace of about 3.5 to 4.5 mph.
key_points: The 23-foot-long trackway contains four three-toed footprints, each about 3 feet long with a 13-foot stride.
The discovery was made in North Dakota's Hell Creek Formation by researchers from the Denver Museum of Nature and Science and Liverpool John Moores University.
High-resolution 3D scanning helped researchers determine the dinosaur was walking at a speed of 3.5 to 4.5 mph.
Three of the footprints are scheduled to be recovered by helicopter and transported to the Denver museum later this year.

title: Can any animal kill a blue whale? At 33 metres long and heavier than a Boeing 737, it is the largest creature ever to have lived but is it vulnerable? | Discover Wildlife
author: Melissa Hobson
content:
In the ocean, different animals have their own unique self-defence strategies to help them survive predators. Some, like crustaceans have hard shells to protect their vulnerable parts. Others go on the offensive; for example, blue-ringed octopuses strike back at attackers with a venomous bite.
Some critters active stealth mode: octopuses blend into their background using camouflage while pygmy sperm whales spurt dark red intestinal fluid into the water, like a smokescreen, to give them a chance to vanish in the confusion.
The largest animal in the world – the blue whale – is protected from most assailants by its sheer size. At up to 33 metres long, these epic animals are longer than a tennis court. Calves weigh around the same as an African elephant and females can grow to around 180,000kg – more than a Boeing 737. It’s no surprise that most animals don’t try to take them on.
Can any animal kill a blue whale?
But there is one species that can overcome a blue whale: orcas. Often considered the ocean’s apex predator, killer whales hunt many other animals, from small fish and salmon to sharks and marine mammals, such as seals, dolphins and whales (depending on their ecotype – different types of killer whales have different diets). Some orcas have even learned how to kill great white sharks – snacking on just their liver and leaving the rest of the carcass.
- “No other predator is able to challenge them” – this deadly, intelligent ocean killer works in a team to stun, submerge and launch at its prey
- At a staggering 33 metres long it's not only the biggest animal in the world today, it is the biggest animal to have ever lived...
Although clever killer whales often pick off weaker and more vulnerable animals, such as whale calves, a pod has been recorded killing an adult blue whale. Scientists came across the incident by accident and were astonished to witness a pod of around 14 killer whales worked together to kill an 18-22m long blue whale, who seemed otherwise healthy.
The huge carcass sank to the seafloor but the killer whales didn’t let that stop their feast: the researchers saw the orcas diving down and returning to the surface with mouthfuls of flesh, sharing their bounty with their pod-mates.
Other animals would have benefited from this kill too. Although other species don’t actively hunt blue whales, many scavengers make the most of the carcass bringing important nutrients down to the seabed. This banquet is an important part of the food web and is known as whale fall.
There’s one other animal that’s capable of killing graceful blue whales: humans. Before commercial whaling was banned, hundreds of thousands of blue whales were killed (nearly 30,000 of those were slaughtered in the 1930-31 season alone). Thankfully, their numbers are now recovering.
summary: While the blue whale is the largest animal to ever live and is protected from most predators by its sheer size, it does have natural and human enemies. Orcas, operating in coordinated pods, are capable of hunting and killing both blue whale calves and healthy adults. Additionally, humans historically decimated blue whale populations through commercial whaling before it was banned, though their numbers are now recovering.
key_points: Blue whales can grow up to 33 metres long and weigh more than a Boeing 737.
Orcas are the only known animal predator capable of killing a blue whale, using teamwork to overcome their massive size.
Researchers have recorded a pod of about 14 killer whales successfully killing an adult blue whale.
Humans were previously responsible for killing hundreds of thousands of blue whales through commercial whaling.
Dead blue whale carcasses, known as whale falls, sink to the seafloor and provide important nutrients to scavengers.

title: Astronomers discover two stars that joined together to form a binary system just 60 years ago
author: Robert Lea
content:
![An ALMA image of IRAS 07299−1651 with the reconstructed orbital trajectories overlaid](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/8yMhrkpxqXLq89RLUoCGB9.png) 
Using the ALMA (Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array) radio telescope, astronomers have watched as two stars come together to form a massive stellar binary. The observations revealed that these stars didn't form from the same collapsing cloud of gas and dust, as most binary stars are assumed to form, but instead came together later in their infancy.
Here on Earth, we are slightly prejudiced by our single sun to view stars as somewhat solitary bodies. However, around half of sun-sized stars in the Milky Way have a companion star. This percentage of stellar partnership rises to around 90% of massive stars. Eventually, these massive stars go supernova and shape their cosmic surroundings. Thus, understanding these binary systems is vital to our understanding of stars and of galaxies in general.
The team behind this research initially observed the still-growing massive stars, or protostars, in the binary system IRAS 07299−1651, located around 5,300 light-years away in 2019. At first, the researchers didn't see anything that suggested these stars didn't form from the same disk-shaped cloud of gas and dust that later fragmented. However, one thing really stood out: the disks of material surrounding and feeding these protostars are oddly misaligned.
Over the course of eight years, the team mapped subtle shifts in the position of the stars using ALMA in addition to the Very Large Array (VLA), as well as infrared images from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Very Large Telescope (VLT).
"For the first time, we were able to watch two massive stars move around one another while they were still being born," team leader Yichen Zhang of Shanghai Jiao Tong University, China, said in a statement.
The team was able to reconstruct the full 3-dimensional structure of IRAS 07299−1651 for the first time, obtaining details about how the stars orbit each other, the way their disks are aligned, and the angle at which they blast jets into space.
"Each telescope revealed a different piece of the puzzle," team member Rubén Fedriani, of the Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía (IAA) in Granada, Spain, said. "The combination of radio and infrared observations provides the most exquisite detail on the formation of this massive protobinary system."
Unexpected chaos
The team's observations took them by surprise. They were expecting these stars to orbit each other in neat, near-circular orbits. Instead, the orbits were found to be highly flattened or "eccentric," almost parabolic.
If the stars had formed from the same disk of material, then even after it fragmented, the individual disks surrounding the stars would be aligned. However, that wasn't the case; the disks are tilted at a sharp angle to each other and to the orbits of the stars.
"It felt like solving a three-dimensional puzzle," team member Yao Wang of Shanghai Jiao Tong University said. "Each new observation added another piece, and eventually the orbit, disks, and jets all came together into a single, coherent picture."
 ![two orange disks with blue jets streaming from their centers](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/FGRoLRHT8f6nkmStdH4nR.jpg) 
The chaotic structure of IRAS 07299−1651, as observed by the team, is difficult to explain if the two stars emerged from the same disk of material.
Instead, the researchers theorize that the two stars were born in individual clouds of gas and dust, before a chance encounter brought the two infant stars and their respective natal cocoons together.
Tracing back the orbits of the stars, the researchers found that this encounter likely occurred around 60 years ago. Considering stars live for billions of years, that is an instant on a cosmic timescale. The disk-shaped pockets of material around the stars have thus far survived the encounter, retaining their well-defined structures.
"This study demonstrates that the early lives of stars can be quite chaotic, with a chance encounter leading to this gravitational dance and stellar coupling," team member Jonathan C. Tan of the University of Technology and the University of Virginia said.
 ![A large yellow sphere next to a smaller red sphere](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/bnpgKtnB9mQWehkyMEGz4b.jpeg) 
What the team can't yet establish is whether these stars are destined to stick together or if they will eventually move apart. Indeed, this fate may not have been sealed yet; interactions with the surrounding gas could determine what shape this system takes in the future.
The team hopes that further observations of IRAS 07299−1651 will help to better understand what the future holds for these stars.
In the meantime, the long-term monitoring approach adopted by the researchers could provide scientists with a powerful new way of investigating other young massive binary systems. This could reveal how common encounters like this are and if more binary systems are composed of stars brought together by chance encounters.
The team's research was published on Tuesday (Sept. 8) in the journal Nature Astronomy.
